title: Genuinely Multipartite Entangled Qudits: One Rule To Link Them All
authors: Rui Andr\'{e} Gon\c{c}alo M. Quinta
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Links of rings offer an intuitive picture of multipartite entanglement. Cutting one ring can free some of the others, just as losing a particle, i.e. tracing it out, can disentangle some of the remaining ones. This analogy classifies multipartite entanglement according to which groups of particles stay entangled when others are lost, a question at the heart of robust quantum networks. However, pure states realizing a given link class were known only in special cases. Here, we close this gap. Recasting link polynomials as hypergraphs, we give an explicit formula for pure qudit states and prove that, for every link class, their entanglement under any pattern of particle loss matches the link exactly. The same construction also controls genuine multipartite entanglement, determining exactly which of the groups that stay entangled are genuinely multipartite entangled, and all of them can be made so. As a consequence, we prove the conjecture that [MATH]-resistant pure qudit states, which stay entangled after the loss of any [MATH] particles but become fully separable after the loss of [MATH], exist for any number of particles and any [MATH].
tldr: The paper constructs explicit pure qudit states realizing arbitrary multipartite entanglement link classes and characterizes their genuine multipartite entanglement under particle loss.
motivation: Link diagrams provide an intuitive classification of multipartite entanglement by which subsets remain entangled after tracing out particles, but pure states realizing general link classes were known only in special cases.
method: The authors recast link polynomials as hypergraphs and derive an explicit formula for pure qudit states whose entanglement under any particle-loss pattern matches a prescribed link class.
result: They prove exact matching for all link classes, determine which surviving groups are genuinely multipartite entangled, show all can be made genuinely multipartite, and prove the existence conjecture for k-resistant pure qudit states for arbitrary particle number and k.
conclusion: This closes a gap in the theory of multipartite entanglement classification and provides flexible constructions relevant to robust entanglement in quantum networks.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the classification of multipartite entanglement in pure qudit states through the lens of link polynomials from knot theory. The authors observe that the way entanglement persists or vanishes when subsets of particles are traced out mirrors the behavior of links when rings are cut. They recast link polynomials as hypergraphs and provide an explicit construction of pure qudit states that realize any given link class. The key result is a proof that for every link class, there exists a pure qudit state whose entanglement under any pattern of particle loss exactly matches the link's structure. Furthermore, the construction controls genuine multipartite entanglement (GME), determining exactly which groups remain genuinely multipartite entangled after losses, and showing that all such groups can be made GME. As a corollary, they prove the conjecture that m-resistant pure qudit states exist for any number of particles and any m: states that remain entangled after loss of any m particles but become fully separable after loss of m+1. The work thus closes a gap between the topological classification of multipartite entanglement and its physical realization in quantum states.

The approach is constructive and general, applicable to any number of particles and any link class, and the proof of the m-resistant conjecture follows from the ability to design states with specific loss-tolerance properties.

title: The Thermodynamic Complexity Of Circuits
authors: Anne Condon, David Doty, Niels Kornerup, David Soloveichik, David Wolpert
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When any physical system executes a logically irreversible (non-injective) step of a computation, the excess heat released over the Landauer limit is an energetic cost that cannot be recovered. In modern computers this cost vastly dwarfs the Landauer cost. Modern stochastic thermodynamics refers to this cost as the ``entropy production'' and has derived fundamental lower bounds on its value. Here we introduce a thermodynamic model of circuits using heat functions and investigate its entropy production, deriving new results on the thermodynamic complexity of circuits. We first show that computing the optimal heat functions for gates in a given circuit (minimizing the entropy production) is PP-complete and multiplicative approximation of those heat functions is NP-hard, but additive approximation admits a polynomial-time randomized algorithm. We give tight bounds for entropy production for certain specific families of circuits (on uniformly distributed inputs): an [MATH]-ary AND tree of depth [MATH] requires [MATH] entropy production, while a serial chain achieves [MATH] in an idealized model, showing an energy-depth tradeoff. The Batcher odd-even mergesort network on [MATH] bits has [MATH] entropy production, asymptotically less than its [MATH] gate count. On random permutations of distinct integers its entropy production is [MATH], asymptotically exceeding the Landauer cost of sorting; but preceding it with Leighton and Plaxton's almost-sorting network reduces the total heat released to [MATH]. Finally, we show how to sort [MATH] values with zero circuit entropy production over any exchangeable input distribution. Our framework also yields streamlined proofs of known results in stochastic thermodynamics on mismatch cost and modularity cost.
tldr: The paper introduces a thermodynamic circuit model based on heat functions and analyzes entropy production to characterize the thermodynamic complexity of irreversible computation.
motivation: Irreversible computational steps dissipate heat beyond the Landauer limit, and modern stochastic thermodynamics provides lower bounds on this entropy production, motivating a circuit-level theory of thermodynamic costs.
method: The authors define heat functions for gates and circuits, study the computational complexity of optimizing them, and derive entropy-production bounds for specific circuit families including AND trees, serial chains, and Batcher's odd-even mergesort.
result: Optimizing heat functions is PP-complete, multiplicative approximation is NP-hard, and additive approximation is achievable in randomized polynomial time; they obtain tight entropy-production bounds exhibiting energy-depth tradeoffs and improved sorting-network costs.
conclusion: The framework provides new thermodynamic complexity results for circuits and streamlined proofs of known stochastic-thermodynamics results on mismatch cost and modularity cost.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper develops a thermodynamic model of Boolean circuits using heat functions to quantify entropy production—the excess heat dissipated beyond the Landauer limit when a circuit performs logically irreversible operations. The authors formalize the problem of minimizing entropy production for a given circuit and analyze its computational complexity, showing that finding optimal heat functions is PP-complete and that multiplicative approximation is NP-hard, while additive approximation admits a polynomial-time randomized algorithm. They then derive tight bounds on entropy production for specific circuit families under uniformly distributed inputs: an n-ary AND tree of depth O(log n) requires Ω(n) entropy production, whereas a serial chain achieves O(1) in an idealized model, revealing an energy-depth tradeoff. For sorting networks, the Batcher odd-even mergesort on n bits has Θ(n) entropy production, asymptotically less than its Θ(n log^2 n) gate count, but on random permutations of distinct integers its entropy production becomes Θ(n log^2 n), exceeding the Landauer cost of sorting; preceding it with Leighton and Plaxton's almost-sorting network reduces total heat to O(n log n). The paper also shows how to sort n values with zero circuit entropy production over any exchangeable input distribution and provides streamlined proofs of known results in stochastic thermodynamics on mismatch cost and modularity cost.

Shows that sorting can be achieved with zero circuit entropy production over any exchangeable input distribution.
Provides streamlined proofs of known results in stochastic thermodynamics, including mismatch cost and modularity cost, within the circuit framework.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors introduce a thermodynamic model where each gate in a circuit is associated with a heat function that specifies the heat dissipated for each input-output transition. Entropy production is defined as the total heat minus the Landauer cost (kT ln 2 per logically irreversible bit operation), and the goal is to minimize this quantity over possible heat functions consistent with the circuit's logical function. They analyze the computational complexity of this optimization problem using reductions from PP-complete and NP-hard problems, and they develop a randomized approximation algorithm based on convex optimization and sampling. For specific circuit families, they construct explicit heat functions and prove lower bounds using information-theoretic arguments and martingale techniques. The analysis of sorting networks leverages known results on almost-sorting and exchangeable distributions to derive asymptotic bounds.
deep_read.results_analysis: The complexity results show that exact minimization of entropy production is PP-complete, meaning it is as hard as counting the number of accepting paths of a nondeterministic Turing machine, and that even multiplicative approximation is NP-hard. However, additive approximation is tractable via a randomized polynomial-time algorithm. For the AND tree, the Ω(n) lower bound implies that any implementation of an n-ary AND with depth O(log n) must dissipate at least a constant times n times the Landauer cost, while a serial chain can achieve O(1) entropy production in an idealized model, highlighting a tradeoff between depth and energy. For sorting, the Batcher network's Θ(n) entropy production on uniform inputs is asymptotically smaller than its Θ(n log^2 n) gates, but on random permutations it becomes Θ(n log^2 n), which exceeds the Landauer cost of sorting (which is Θ(n log n) for comparison-based sorting). Precomposing with the Leighton-Plaxton almost-sorting network reduces the total heat to O(n log n), matching the Landauer cost up to constants. The zero-entropy sorting result for exchangeable distributions is particularly striking, as it shows that no excess heat is necessary when the input distribution is symmetric.

Derives tight asymptotic bounds for concrete circuit families, offering practical implications for energy-efficient computing.

The concepts of entropy production, mismatch cost, and modularity cost are central to stochastic thermodynamics, which underpins the study of quantum thermodynamic systems. The paper is well-structured and the proofs appear sound, making it a valuable addition to the literature.

title: Induced Bell-CHSH Observables In The Fewster-Verch Measurement Scheme
authors: M. S. Guimaraes, I. Roditi, S. P. Sorella
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Summers-Werner theorem shows that the vacuum of a relativistic quantum field theory violates the Bell-CHSH inequality maximally on complementary wedges, but it is an existence statement: it exhibits neither the observables nor an apparatus that measures them. We give an explicit operator-level realization within the Fewster-Verch measurement framework, obtaining dichotomic Bell observables of a free Majorana field in [MATH] dimensions as observables induced by local couplings to Majorana probes. The induced system smearing factorizes exactly as [MATH], so its support is controlled by the compactly supported coupling profile [MATH]; dichotomy is imposed by calibrating and normalizing the induced smearings rather than required of the probe observable; and a probe-only normal ordering yields the product of Alice's and Bob's induced bilinears, which the non-multiplicative induced map alone does not provide. Under explicit attainability hypotheses the induced observables saturate the Tsirelson bound in a state prepared from the vacuum. The construction extends to coupled scalar fields.
tldr: The paper gives an explicit operator-level realization of Bell-CHSH observables for a free Majorana field within the Fewster-Verch measurement framework, induced by local couplings to probe systems.
motivation: The Summers-Werner theorem establishes maximal vacuum Bell-CHSH violation on complementary wedges but only as an existence result, without constructing the observables or measuring apparatus; this work aims to fill that gap.
method: Using the Fewster-Verch measurement scheme, the authors induce dichotomic Bell observables in a free Majorana field through local couplings to Majorana probes, with controlled smearing profiles and probe-only normal ordering to obtain Alice-Bob bilinear products.
result: The induced observables factorize exactly, have support controlled by the coupling profile, and, under explicit attainability hypotheses, saturate the Tsirelson bound in a state prepared from the vacuum; the construction extends to coupled scalar fields.
conclusion: This provides a concrete measurement-theoretic realization of Bell nonlocality in relativistic quantum field theory, moving beyond existence proofs toward explicit observable-level constructions.

They consider a free Majorana field in 1+1 dimensions and construct dichotomic Bell observables as observables induced by local couplings to Majorana probe fields. The induced system smearing factorizes exactly as f_h = k b_{λ,h}, where k is a compactly supported coupling profile controlling the support, and b_{λ,h} is a function that ensures dichotomy after calibration and normalization. The construction shows that dichotomy is imposed by calibrating and normalizing the induced smearings rather than being required of the probe observable. A probe-only normal ordering yields the product of Alice's and Bob's induced bilinears, which the non-multiplicative induced map alone does not provide. Under explicit attainability hypotheses, the induced observables saturate the Tsirelson bound in a state prepared from the vacuum. The construction is also extended to coupled scalar fields.

title: Admissible Subspaces For The Collective Haar Twirl: Schur-Weyl Classification And Heredity Under Tensor-Factor Reduction
authors: Sayantan Ganguly
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum private broadcasting () asks whether a quantum message can be encrypted once, broadcast to several recipients, and decrypted locally while the joint ciphertext reveals no plaintext information. Broadbent, Gonz\'alez-Guill\'en, and Schuknecht showed that the full tensor-power space \(\mathcal H_d^{\otimes t}\) is generally unsuitable for , identified \(^t(\mathcal H_d)\) as a natural plaintext space, introduced symmetric unitary \(t\)-designs, and asked which other subspaces support private broadcast. Using Schur-Weyl duality, we classify all subspaces \(\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal H_d^{\otimes t}\) on which the collective Haar twirl \(\mathcal T^{(t)}\) is a replacement channel. Precisely, every Schur-Weyl block weight must be independent of the encoded state, and in each active block \(V_\lambda\otimes W_\lambda\), the reduced state on the multiplicity space \(W_\lambda\) must be fixed. This yields explicit two-block and general multiblock constructions and realizes the classification as the Schur-Weyl form of the Knill-Laflamme conditions for a complementary channel of \(\mathcal T^{(t)}\). We also introduce a canonical reduction under deletion of a recipient and characterize privacy heredity, design heredity, and -heredity for exact restricted designs. The symmetric tower is fully -hereditary, whereas the antisymmetric tower is fully privacy-hereditary and is design-hereditary from level \(s\) to \(s-1\) exactly when \(s\leq(d+1)/2\). For canonical carriers in arbitrary Schur-Weyl blocks, hereditary reduction is governed by multiplicity-free branching along the Young graph and inclusion of the associated Peter-Weyl coefficient spaces.
tldr: The paper classifies subspaces of tensor-power Hilbert spaces on which the collective Haar twirl acts as a replacement channel, enabling quantum private broadcasting via Schur-Weyl duality.
motivation: Quantum private broadcasting asks whether a quantum message can be encrypted once and broadcast to multiple recipients while revealing no plaintext information jointly, and prior work left open which subspaces support this primitive.
method: Using Schur-Weyl duality, the authors analyze the collective Haar twirl and derive conditions on Schur-Weyl block weights and multiplicity-space reduced states, connecting the classification to Knill-Laflamme conditions for a complementary channel and studying heredity under recipient deletion.
result: They classify admissible subspaces via block-weight independence and fixed multiplicity-space states, give explicit two-block and multiblock constructions, and characterize privacy, design, and related heredity properties, including full heredity of symmetric and antisymmetric towers under specific conditions.
conclusion: The work provides a representation-theoretic foundation for identifying subspaces suitable for quantum private broadcasting and clarifies hereditary behavior under tensor-factor reduction.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper addresses the problem of quantum private broadcasting (QPB), which asks whether a quantum state can be encrypted once, broadcast to multiple recipients, and decrypted locally such that the joint ciphertext reveals no information about the plaintext. Prior work by Broadbent, González-Guillén, and Schuknecht showed that the full tensor-power space H_d^{⊗t} is generally unsuitable for QPB, identified the symmetric subspace Sym^t(H_d) as a natural plaintext space, and introduced symmetric unitary t-designs. They left open the classification of other subspaces that support private broadcast. The present paper uses Schur-Weyl duality to classify all subspaces S ⊆ H_d^{⊗t} on which the collective Haar twirl T^{(t)} acts as a replacement channel. The classification requires that every Schur-Weyl block weight be independent of the encoded state and that, within each active block V_λ ⊗ W_λ, the reduced state on the multiplicity space W_λ be fixed. The authors provide explicit two-block and general multiblock constructions and interpret the classification as the Schur-Weyl form of the Knill-Laflamme conditions for a complementary channel of T^{(t)}. They also introduce a canonical reduction under deletion of a recipient and characterize privacy heredity, design heredity, and QPB-heredity for exact restricted designs. Notably, the symmetric tower is fully QPB-hereditary, while the antisymmetric tower is fully privacy-hereditary and design-hereditary from level s to s-1 exactly when s ≤ (d+1)/2. For canonical carriers in arbitrary Schur-Weyl blocks, hereditary reduction is governed by multiplicity-free branching along the Young graph and inclusion of associated Peter-Weyl coefficient spaces.
key_contributions: Complete classification of subspaces S ⊆ H_d^{⊗t} on which the collective Haar twirl T^{(t)} is a replacement channel, using Schur-Weyl duality: the condition is that each Schur-Weyl block weight is state-independent and the reduced state on each active multiplicity space W_λ is fixed.
Explicit construction of two-block and general multiblock subspaces that support QPB, going beyond the symmetric subspace previously identified.
Identification of the classification as the Schur-Weyl form of the Knill-Laflamme conditions for a complementary channel of T^{(t)}, linking QPB to quantum error correction.
Introduction of a canonical reduction under deletion of a recipient and characterization of privacy heredity, design heredity, and QPB-heredity for exact restricted designs.

Proof that the symmetric tower is fully QPB-hereditary, the antisymmetric tower is fully privacy-hereditary, and design heredity from level s to s-1 holds exactly when s ≤ (d+1)/2; for general Schur-Weyl blocks, hereditary reduction is governed by multiplicity-free branching along the Young graph and inclusion of Peter-Weyl coefficient spaces.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper relies heavily on Schur-Weyl duality, which decomposes the tensor power space H_d^{⊗t} under the joint action of the unitary group U(d) and the symmetric group S_t. This decomposition allows the authors to analyze the collective Haar twirl T^{(t)} block by block. The key technical step is to characterize when T^{(t)} acts as a replacement channel on a subspace S, which requires that the twirl destroys all information about the encoded state. By examining the reduced states on the multiplicity spaces W_λ, the authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions for QPB. They then construct explicit examples of subspaces satisfying these conditions, including two-block and multiblock constructions. The hereditary analysis uses the Young graph and branching rules to study how properties behave under deletion of a recipient, which corresponds to restricting the subspace to a smaller tensor power. The connection to Knill-Laflamme conditions is established by identifying the twirl as a complementary channel and applying the standard error-correction criteria.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is a complete classification: a subspace S supports QPB if and only if for each Schur-Weyl block λ, the weight p_λ = Tr(P_λ ρ) is independent of the encoded state ρ, and the reduced state on the multiplicity space W_λ is fixed (i.e., independent of ρ). This generalizes the known result for the symmetric subspace, where only the trivial representation of S_t appears. The authors provide explicit constructions: for two blocks, they show that any subspace of the form (V_λ ⊗ W_λ) ⊕ (V_μ ⊗ W_μ) with appropriate fixed states on W_λ and W_μ works. For multiblock, similar conditions apply. The hereditary results are precise: the symmetric tower (all symmetric powers) is fully QPB-hereditary, meaning any reduction by deleting recipients preserves QPB. The antisymmetric tower is fully privacy-hereditary but design-hereditary only up to level s ≤ (d+1)/2. For general blocks, heredity is governed by multiplicity-free branching, which imposes strong constraints. These results are significant because they identify a rich family of QPB-compatible subspaces beyond the symmetric one and clarify the limitations of hereditary properties.
strengths: The use of Schur-Weyl duality provides a clean and powerful framework for classifying QPB subspaces, yielding a complete and explicit characterization.
The connection to Knill-Laflamme conditions for complementary channels bridges QPB with quantum error correction, offering new insights and potential tools.
The hereditary analysis is thorough, with precise thresholds (e.g., s ≤ (d+1)/2) and clear identification of which towers are hereditary, which is valuable for understanding scalability.
The paper provides explicit constructions (two-block, multiblock) that make the classification concrete and applicable.
limitations: The classification assumes exact QPB (perfect privacy and decryption), whereas practical applications may require approximate or noisy versions; the paper does not address robustness.
The hereditary analysis is restricted to exact restricted designs and canonical carriers; it is unclear how these results extend to more general subspaces or approximate designs.
The paper focuses on the collective Haar twirl and symmetric unitary t-designs; other encryption schemes or twirls are not considered, which may limit the generality of the conclusions.

The classification of subspaces supporting QPB advances the understanding of quantum encryption and broadcasting, which are fundamental primitives in quantum network security. title: Exact Operator Bounds On Leggett-Garg Violations
authors: Rathindra Nath Das, Arnab Kundu, Nemai Chandra Sarkar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Leggett-Garg (LG) inequalities test whether correlations measured at different times admit a positive joint probability distribution over histories. A violation requires negative values in any joint quasiprobability distribution reproducing those correlations, but such distributions can have negative values even without a violation. Spacetime density kernels extend the density-matrix description to multiple times and are used to study timelike entanglement. We establish a universal bound that relates LG violations to their negative eigenvalue weight. For LG tests involving any number of measurements, we determine the least compatible kernel negativity through an exact relation valid for any system dimension, initial state, dynamics, or measurement rule. This minimum is nonzero if and only if at least one LG inequality is violated. Three-time L\"uders LG tests certify at most one eighth of negativity, whereas measurements resolving individual spin levels can approach one half. Including additional incompatible qubit observables gives a further exact minimum that can exceed the LG-only ceiling without increasing the LG violation.

motivation: Leggett-Garg inequalities test whether temporal correlations admit a classical joint probability description, but quasiprobability negativity can occur without an LG violation; the authors aim to characterize the minimal kernel negativity required for such violations.
method: They formulate LG tests using spacetime density kernels and establish universal exact relations between LG violation and negative eigenvalue weight, including multi-time and multi-observable scenarios.
result: The minimum kernel negativity is nonzero iff at least one LG inequality is violated; three-time Lueders tests certify at most one eighth of negativity, while spin-level-resolving measurements can approach one half, and additional incompatible qubit observables yield further exact minima.
conclusion: The work provides a precise operator-level link between temporal nonclassicality, quasiprobability negativity, and Leggett-Garg violations, clarifying the resource content of timelike quantum correlations.

title: Krylov Geometry And Optimal Recovery Under Uncertain Coherent Noise
authors: Abhishek Chowdhury
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recovery from a coherent rotation with an unobserved angle depends on both the encoding and what calibration reveals about the noise. The optimal worst-input error lies between one and [MATH] times that infidelity at leading order, for logical dimension [MATH]. When the angle distribution is unknown, we optimize one decoder for every distribution compatible with the calibration. When spectral and calibration frequencies are integer multiples of a common frequency, moment positivity turns this into an exact finite optimization. Small measured means can still allow rare finite rotations. If the sole calibration datum is [MATH], with [MATH] the wrapped rotation phase at that common frequency, the optimal worst-prior infidelity is [MATH] exactly when generator powers through degree [MATH] are correctable. title: Ground-state Spaces Of Generalized Stabilizer Codes
authors: Cathy Cheng, Nigel Higson, Danilo Polo Ojito, Emil Prodan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33221v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we determine the complete ground-state spaces for a broad class of generalized stabilizer quantum models defined over CW-decompositions of non-compact manifolds of arbitrary dimensions and topological type. We introduce a [MATH]-algebraic framework in which the quantum spin algebra [MATH] is realized as the twisted group [MATH]-algebra of an infinite discrete Pauli module [MATH] endowed with a symplectic structure. We establish a correspondence between stabilizer models and isotropic subgroups of [MATH]: Every Lagrangian extension of such a subgroup determines a [MATH]-diagonal of [MATH], whose Weyl groupoid encodes the dynamics through a continuous 1-cocycle. This realization yields an explicit family of extremal ground-states for every admissible Lagrangian model, together with their decomposition into sectors. When the sector space is [MATH], this gives a complete characterization of the ground-state spaces. We also prove that every Lagrangian stabilizer model admits a unique frustration-free ground state with a spectral gap. Our framework applies in arbitrary dimension, including higher abelian quantum doubles, homological codes, and a broad class of stabilizer models.

title: Twirled And Swirled Worlds: A Compositional Approach
authors: Sina Soltani, Thomas D. Galley, Marco Erba, John H. Selby
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Twirled and swirled worlds describe generalised probabilistic theories (GPTs) restricted by symmetry-imposed superselection rules. We extend these constructions to a fully compositional setting for finite-dimensional GPTs and compact groups, treating states, effects, and multipartite transformations uniformly as processes. We distinguish system actions from process-space actions. We define actions on a theory as a whole by requiring the corresponding process-space actions to respect sequential and parallel composition. Averaging physical theory actions defines twirling, while averaging nonphysical theory actions defines swirling. We show that invariant subtheories might not satisfy process tomography, and establish conditions under which they do, involving invariant dynamically faithful states or internal classical reference frames. For locally tomographic parent theories, we prove that every theory symmetry admits a representation by linear system actions and that the invariant subtheory satisfies process tomography. An invariant multipartite process space fails local tomography if and only if some bipartition has sides sharing a non-trivial irreducible representation. We characterise when ancillary systems are necessary, which representations they must carry, and when entanglement is required for ancilla-free process tomography. We develop a framework for unifying twirled subtheories and extend incoherent simulations to compact groups. Finally, we recover bilocal classical theory as a twirled subtheory of classical theory and real quantum theory as a swirled subtheory of complex quantum theory, deriving their tomographic properties from their representation structure.
tldr: The paper extends twirled and swirled generalised probabilistic theory constructions to a fully compositional framework, characterising invariant subtheories and their process-tomography properties via group representation theory.
motivation: Symmetry-restricted GPTs called twirled and swirled worlds require a compositional formulation to uniformly treat states, effects, and multipartite transformations, and to understand when invariant subtheories remain tomographically well behaved.
method: The authors model states, effects, and transformations as processes, distinguish system actions from process-space actions, define theory-level actions respecting sequential and parallel composition, and use averaging over physical versus nonphysical actions to define twirling and swirling.
result: They show invariant subtheories may fail process tomography, give conditions for tomography via invariant dynamically faithful states or internal classical reference frames, prove representation theorems for locally tomographic parent theories, and characterise when ancillas or entanglement are necessary.
conclusion: The framework unifies twirled subtheories, extends incoherent simulations to compact groups, and recovers bilocal classical theory and real quantum theory as twirled/swirled subtheories with tomographic properties derived from representation structure.

title: Distributional Statistics Of Nonequilibrium
authors: Harrison Hartle, Aanjaneya Kumar, David H. Wolpert
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33383v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a reference modeling framework for random probability distributions subject to constraints. Generalizing the hyperensemble approach of Crooks, we formulate Jaynesian priors of maximal uncertainty over the unit simplex of categorical distributions. This framework is entirely general, but we primarily investigate models with constraints on physically relevant quantities, namely, average energy and Shannon entropy. A constraint on the exact value of average energy uniquely determines a Boltzmann-Gibbs equilibrium, but also defines a hyperplanar subset of the probability simplex consisting of all distributions with that value of average energy. The associated hyperensemble has a uniform probability density across all such distributions, regardless of distance to equilibrium. Such reference models make predictions of generic nonequilibrium properties such as the mean and modal microstate distributions and the expected free energy of a random distribution, which we examine analytically and via exact sampling algorithms. Moreover, introducing constraints on Shannon entropy permits parametric access to tunably nonequilibrium regimes. The approach follows conventional Jaynesian modeling logic and is compatible with standard Bayesian inference, and reduces to Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics when Shannon entropy is maximized. We examine the physical predictions of this scheme, and demonstrate its wide compatibility with other approaches to nonequilibrium modeling. We illustrate the framework in three scenarios: (i) comparison to superstatistics quasi-equilibrium modeling, (ii) generation of random nonequilibrium steady states, and (iii) Bayesian inference under a prior hyperensemble. We highlight numerous prospects for theoretical extensions and empirical application.
tldr: The paper develops a Jaynesian hyperensemble framework for random probability distributions under constraints on average energy and Shannon entropy, yielding reference models for nonequilibrium statistics.

title: Path-Distinguishability Gaps At Fixed Visibility In Noisy Qubit Interferometers
authors: Mohd Asad Siddiqui
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The wave--particle duality relation bounds visibility and path distinguishability but does not determine their attainable values in a fixed noisy interferometer. We characterize the complete attainable region for a two-path interferometer with a qubit marker, varying the marker input while fixing the source, preparation channel, path-dependent interaction, and subsequent marker channel. At each feasible fringe visibility, the Helstrom-optimal distinguishabilities form at most two closed intervals, which can be separated by a gap. The intervals arise from opposite axial marker polarizations with the same fringe-amplitude modulus. Fixing the complex fringe amplitude instead gives a connected interval; for balanced original-path discrimination, a gap requires nonunital marker preparation. For a balanced pure source, relative [MATH] rotations, and no subsequent marker noise, we obtain a necessary and sufficient geometric criterion for a gap under some rotation axis perpendicular to the preparation displacement. Explicit channels and a time-independent Lindblad realization show how the gap depends on preparation geometry and evolution, with exact onset and optimization formulas at fixed fractional visibility. We also give sufficient bounds for excluding distinguishability intervals under calibrated finite-resolution errors.

motivation: Wave-particle duality bounds visibility and path distinguishability but does not specify which pairs are attainable in a given noisy interferometer, so the authors aim to map the full achievable region under fixed source, channels, and interactions.
method: They vary the qubit marker input while holding the interferometer setup fixed, derive the structure of optimal distinguishability intervals as a function of visibility, and analyze gap conditions using marker polarization, nonunital preparation, geometric criteria, and explicit Lindblad channel realizations.
result: At fixed feasible visibility, optimal distinguishabilities form at most two closed intervals that can be separated by a gap; fixing complex fringe amplitude instead yields a connected interval, and for balanced pure sources a geometric criterion for gapped behavior is obtained under specified rotation and noise conditions.
conclusion: The work provides exact onset and optimization formulas for distinguishability gaps at fixed fractional visibility and gives sufficient bounds for excluding intervals under calibrated finite-resolution errors, clarifying how preparation geometry and evolution constrain wave-particle duality in noisy interferometers.

title: When Is A Bosonic Operator A Hamiltonian?
authors: Felix Fischer, Hermann Schulz-Baldes, Daniel Burgarth, Davide Lonigro
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hermitian polynomials in the quadrature operators [MATH] and [MATH] are the basic ingredients of continuous-variable quantum information, and increasingly exotic ones are now routinely engineered in superconducting circuits and trapped ions. However, such a polynomial need not define unique quantum dynamics: it may define exactly one, none, or an infinite family of physically distinct ones. Such obstructions are invisible to algebraic arguments and can compromise finite-dimensional truncations, which may fail to converge or silently converge to the wrong dynamics. We develop a method, implemented as an algorithm, which decides which case occurs, and how large the family is, from the coefficients alone, with no functional-analytic input from the user. For Gaussian operators the answer is always one; for non-Gaussian ones, a regime continuous-variable quantum computing cannot do without, the other outcomes occur already for simple and physically natural Hamiltonians. We apply the algorithm to operators drawn from the recent literature.
tldr: The paper develops an algorithmic criterion for deciding whether a Hermitian polynomial in bosonic quadrature operators uniquely defines quantum dynamics, has no dynamics, or has infinitely many physically distinct Hamiltonian generators.
motivation: Continuous-variable quantum information routinely engineers increasingly exotic Hermitian polynomials in quadrature operators, but such operators need not define unique quantum dynamics; algebraic manipulations and finite-dimensional truncations can miss domain-related obstructions and silently converge to incorrect dynamics.
method: The authors formulate the problem in terms of operator domains and self-adjoint extensions, then derive an algorithm that uses only the polynomial coefficients to classify the number of physically distinct Hamiltonian dynamics and the size of the family.
result: For Gaussian operators the dynamics are always unique, while for non-Gaussian operators all outcomes can occur already for simple physically natural Hamiltonians; the algorithm is applied to operators from the recent literature.
conclusion: The work exposes a hidden foundational issue in continuous-variable quantum information and provides a practical coefficient-based test to avoid incorrect finite-dimensional truncations or ambiguous Hamiltonian dynamics.

These obstructions are invisible to algebraic manipulations and can cause finite-dimensional truncations to fail to converge or to converge to the wrong dynamics. The authors develop a method, implemented as an algorithm, that decides from the polynomial coefficients alone which case occurs and, in the infinite-family case, determines the size of the family (i.e., the deficiency indices). The algorithm requires no functional-analytic input from the user. For Gaussian operators (quadratic polynomials), the answer is always one (essential self-adjointness), but for non-Gaussian operators—essential for universal CV quantum computing—the other outcomes already occur for simple and physically natural Hamiltonians. The authors apply the algorithm to operators drawn from recent literature, demonstrating its practical relevance.

title: Junction Hook Errors In The Color Code
authors: Margaret Martonosi Salahedeen Issa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33347v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Color-dependent syndrome extraction schedules have been proposed to mitigate hook errors in the triangular color code. Recent work by Kishony and Fowler (arXiv:2603.28852) identifies distance-reducing hook errors by the type of anyon for which they provide a shortcut and chooses the CNOT ordering for stabilizers of each color to avoid these errors. We identify an additional class of distance-reducing hooks, which we call junction hook errors, that is not captured by this classification. The two data qubits of a junction hook error terminate anyon strings of two different colors at the point where the three colored strings of a logical operator meet, which we call the junction. As such, the hook error does not correspond to a single type of anyon, yet it still reduces the distance. For distances [MATH], we verify that every non-corner plaquette admits a scheduled hook error that, together with [MATH] single data qubit faults, produces an undetectable logical error using [MATH] faults. Each of these is a junction hook error. Because of this, every stabilizer, including those in the bulk, still requires additional protection from hook errors (such as flag qubits) to restore the full circuit-level distance with this schedule. A minimum weight logical operator has at most one junction, however, so junction hook errors cannot accumulate on one minimum weight logical operator in the way that single-color malign hook errors can. This helps explain why the schedule still improves the circuit-level distance to [MATH], rather than the [MATH] distance associated with spatially uniform color code scheduling.

motivation: Color-dependent syndrome extraction schedules were proposed to suppress hook errors in the triangular color code, but existing classifications based on anyon type do not capture all distance-reducing faults.
method: The authors analyze hook errors arising from CNOT ordering in stabilizer measurements and classify a new type that terminates anyon strings of different colors at a junction of a logical operator.
result: For a range of distances, every non-corner plaquette admits a scheduled junction hook error that, together with single data-qubit faults, produces an undetectable logical error using fewer faults than the target distance.
conclusion: Junction hook errors mean that bulk stabilizers still require additional protection such as flag qubits for full circuit-level distance, but they cannot accumulate on a minimum-weight logical operator as single-color malign hook errors can, explaining the observed distance improvement.

Each of these is a junction hook error. Consequently, every stabilizer, including bulk ones, still requires additional protection (e.g., flag qubits) to restore full circuit-level distance with this schedule. title: Variational Quantum Optimization Of Noisy Polarization Qubit Experiments
authors: Timur Javid, Brian Doolittle, Colin P. Lualdi, Brittany Conner, Michael Vayninger, Eric Chitambar, Paul G. Kwiat
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum networking enables advanced communication protocols, distributed quantum computing, and enhanced sensing. These applications are often hindered by current realizations of quantum network nodes, which utilize noisy and imperfect hardware. Here, we apply variational optimization to counteract the effects of such imperfections. We parameterize network protocols for use with variational methods and then use these methods to optimize simple prepare-and-measure protocols on an optical testbed as a proof-of-principle demonstration. We demonstrate automated polarization compensation, achieving results comparable to conventional methods. We also analyze the effects of hardware imperfections and dark counts on the performance of our optimizations. We compare the performance of various gradient estimation methods and propose natural extensions, including further improvements through the use of global optimization and hybrid gradient estimation methods, as well as the application of variational optimization to nodes deployed on fiber networks.

motivation: Quantum network nodes currently suffer from noisy and imperfect hardware, which limits advanced communication, distributed computing, and sensing applications.
method: The authors parameterize network protocols for variational methods and optimize them on an optical testbed, comparing gradient-estimation approaches and analyzing hardware imperfections and dark counts.
result: They demonstrate automated polarization compensation with performance comparable to conventional methods and characterize how imperfections and dark counts affect variational optimization.
conclusion: Variational optimization is a viable proof-of-principle tool for improving noisy polarization-qubit network-node experiments, with possible extensions to global optimization, hybrid gradient methods, and deployed fiber networks.

title: Large Spin Large Deviations For Interacting Particle Systems
authors: Tomohiro Sasamoto Cristian Giardin\`a
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a novel framework for analyzing the sample-path large deviations of interacting particle systems directly on a lattice by considering a large-spin limit ([MATH]). Through an appropriate scaling of variables, the process concentrates around its deterministic trajectory, governed by the lattice diffusion equation. We quantify the exponential cost of observing atypical trajectories by explicitly computing the path-space large deviation rate function from the scaled microscopic generator, based on a theory due to Feng and Kurtz. The rate function is described in terms of a Hamiltonian on a lattice in terms of classical spin variables. Notably, for our main model, the symmetric harmonic process, the corresponding Hamiltonian is identified with the classical integrable non-compact Ishimori spin chain. Furthermore, we show that our large spin large deviation theory is fully consistent with traditional Macroscopic Fluctuation Theory (MFT), smoothly recovering the standard MFT Hamiltonian in the spatial continuous limit. We also perform a Poisson-noise Martin--Siggia--Rose (MSR) computation to derive the non-linear lattice Hamiltonian directly from microscopic dynamics, use a relative entropy argument to obtain the density-current action, and establish the lattice fluctuation theorem alongside its symmetry origin. Overall, our framework provides a naturally regularized, lattice analogue of MFT that circumvents spatial ultraviolet singularities and possible continuous density blow-ups. We also apply our new scheme to partial symmetric exclusion process, symmetric inclusion processes, Brownian energy process and integrable heat conduction model, showing how their large-deviation Hamiltonians relate to classical compact and non-compact spin chains.

title: Post-Quantum Perfect Zero-Knowledge Arguments For Np From Any One-Way Permutation
authors: Fr\'ed\'eric Dupuis, R\'emi Ligez, Khaireddine Medhioub, Louis Salvail, Louis-Charles Thibodeau
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we show for the first time that post-quantum one-way permutations are sufficient for perfect zero-knowledge classical arguments for all of NP with security guaranteed against quantum adversaries. We first establish that Naor, Ostrovsky,Venkatesen, and Yung's bit commitment scheme built from any permutation using interactive hashing, called the NOVY scheme, is sum-binding and collapse-binding against quantum polynomial-time committers provided the permutation is post-quantum one-way. We then show that the collapse-binding property of the NOVY scheme allows for Blum's perfect zero-knowledge argument for HAMCYCLE to remain so exactly as it stands against quantum adversaries.

method: The authors prove that the NOVY bit commitment scheme from any permutation is sum-binding and collapse-binding against quantum committers if the permutation is post-quantum one-way, then apply collapse-binding to Blum's perfect zero-knowledge argument for HAMCYCLE.
result: They obtain the first construction of perfect zero-knowledge classical arguments for NP from post-quantum one-way permutations with security against quantum adversaries.

title: Competing Fault Histories In Lattice-Surgery Decoding
authors: Niharika Verma
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Different physical faults can produce the same detector record while carrying opposite logical labels. We investigate the consequence of this ambiguity for a lattice surgery parity measurement. In a distance-three merge--split circuit, single-gate faults compete with reset/readout pairs on three complete syndromes. Full-syndrome probabilities give a simultaneous 95\% lower confidence bound of [MATH] parts per million on the cost of retaining the selected single-fault decisions at one noise point. Changing those decisions is harmful at low noise and beneficial at higher noise. To test the physical explanation, we attenuate eight implicated channels and compare the change in override effect with a matched non-target suppression. The two interventions change the decoder effect differently, resolving a contribution associated with those locations. Likelihood predictions fixed before sampling then select useful decisions under mixed Pauli noise and after extending preparation and recovery. The latter test gives a reduction of [MATH] parts per million, with simultaneous 95\% bounds [MATH]. The mechanism is limited in scope: the revised decisions give up certain single-fault corrections, and under the same witness-selection rule no candidate is identified in the fully expanded distance-five circuit. These results connect a finite-noise decoding trade-off to specific physical channels and test how far that explanation can be used to predict logical-parity performance.

conclusion: The trade-off is real but limited in scope: the revised decisions sacrifice some single-fault corrections, and under the same witness-selection rule no candidate is found in the distance-five circuit, bounding how far this physical explanation generalizes.

title: Task-Directed Spectral Design For Local Quantum Tomography
authors: Nir Sharon Guy Hay
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many tomography tasks require only a low-dimensional function of the state. We study local pure-state tomography under projective-fidelity access when a parametric model, a credible center, and a differentiable downstream task are known before acquisition. The pullback Fubini--Study metric and the task metric define coordinate-invariant generalized eigendirections, which we realize as a fixed library of geodesic fidelity probes. We prove two optimality results: the probe aligned with a task coordinate is its unique variance-minimizing location up to orientation, and, when prior and measurement information are diagonal in this basis, a diminishing-return greedy rule exactly minimizes the integer-budget local task-variance surrogate over the spectral library. Under common per-shot information and the stated large-budget condition, the absolute and relative gaps to arbitrary probe directions are respectively \(O(B^{-3})\) and \(O(B^{-2})\). A closed-form local estimator is followed by a task-metric localization projection that cannot increase quadratic task loss when localization holds. In six-qubit numerical experiments, the Schmidt-spectrum design activates only one or two settings and has lower mean task error than the post hoc best adaptive results across all tested dimensions and copy budgets. For full-state tomography, it likewise has lower mean infidelity throughout the tested local regime. The fixed batch uses no feedback loops and far fewer settings; under the illustrative latency model, its acquisition cost is roughly three to four orders of magnitude lower than that of the adaptive methods.

The numerical experiments are limited to six qubits and specific models (Schmidt spectrum); scalability to larger systems and other parameterizations is not demonstrated. The latency model for cost comparison is illustrative and may not reflect real hardware constraints.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to quantum physics, particularly quantum state tomography and quantum information theory. It introduces geometric tools (Fubini-Study metric, generalized eigendecomposition) that are central to quantum information geometry. The focus on local tomography with prior information and task-specific metrics connects to problems in quantum metrology and parameter estimation, where the goal is to estimate a function of the state rather than the full state. The fixed-batch probe design and optimality results could inform experimental protocols for near-term quantum devices, where adaptive feedback is costly. Additionally, the use of the task metric to define relevant directions parallels ideas in quantum machine learning and variational quantum algorithms, where the loss function landscape determines relevant parameter directions.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper presents a novel and rigorous approach to local pure-state tomography by leveraging geometric insights to design fixed, non-adaptive probe libraries. The theoretical results are strong, providing optimality guarantees and asymptotic scaling, and the numerical experiments support the practical advantages. The work is significant for its potential to simplify and speed up tomography in scenarios where prior information and a specific task are available. However, the reliance on local assumptions and diagonal conditions limits its generality, and further validation on larger systems and diverse models is needed. Overall, it is a high-quality contribution that bridges quantum information geometry and practical tomography, with clear implications for experimental quantum physics.

title: Direct Tests Of Conformal Symmetry With Rydberg Atoms: Assessment And Proposals
authors: Slava Rychkov Junchen Rong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a direct test of conformal symmetry using Rydberg-atom arrays. By arranging the atoms on a circle and measuring equal-time two-point correlation functions, the characteristic functional form predicted by conformal field theory can be tested directly. We estimate the number of experimental snapshots required to resolve this behavior with sufficient statistical precision. We further optimize the time-dependent ramp profile of the Rabi frequency~[MATH] and detuning~[MATH] used to prepare the target critical state adiabatically. The optimized profile achieves higher fidelity over much shorter evolution times than those employed in previous experiments. Taken together, these results suggest that a direct experimental test of conformal symmetry is feasible with current Rydberg-atom technology.
tldr: The authors propose and assess a Rydberg-atom-array experiment that measures equal-time two-point correlations on a circular lattice to directly test the functional form of conformal field theory predictions, and optimize the adiabatic ramp of Rabi frequency and detuning needed to prepare the critical state.
motivation: Conformal symmetry underlies much of modern theoretical physics but has rarely been tested directly in a controlled quantum simulator; Rydberg arrays with tunable van der Waals interactions offer a natural platform for realizing a critical (conformal) state.
method: Atoms are arranged on a circle and equal-time two-point correlators are extracted from snapshots, with a statistical estimate of the number of measurements required; the time-dependent Rabi frequency and detuning profiles are numerically optimized to maximise ground-state fidelity at short evolution times.
result: The estimated snapshot counts needed to resolve the CFT scaling form are within experimental reach, and the optimized ramp achieves higher fidelity in much shorter times than previous protocols.
conclusion: A direct experimental test of conformal symmetry appears feasible with current Rydberg-atom technology, though the work is primarily a quantum-simulation/CFT proposal rather than a contribution to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A New Non-Affine Family In The Karlsson-Szollosi Intersection
authors: Andr\'e Ranchin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that [MATH] up to standard Hadamard equivalence, where [MATH] is a new non-affine one-parameter family of complex Hadamard matrices. This demonstrates that the intersection of the two-parameter Hadamard families of Karlsson and Sz\"ollsi is strictly larger than the known affine Di curve [MATH]. Our new parametrisation of the Sz\"ollsi family [MATH] in Karlsson coordinates and our constructive classification of the Karlsson-Sz\"ollsi intersection shed light on the intersection of block-reducible forms and hypocycloid constraints. This may support the search for mutually unbiased bases in six dimensions.
tldr: The paper constructs a new non-affine one-parameter family of complex Hadamard matrices in the Karlsson-Szollosi intersection, potentially aiding the search for mutually unbiased bases in dimension six.
motivation: Complex Hadamard matrices and mutually unbiased bases are relevant to quantum information foundations, but the paper is primarily a mathematical classification result about specific Hadamard families.
method: The author introduces a new parametrisation of the Szollosi family in Karlsson coordinates and gives a constructive classification of the Karlsson-Szollosi intersection, identifying a non-affine family up to Hadamard equivalence.
result: The Karlsson-Szollosi intersection is shown to be strictly larger than the known affine Di curve, revealing new non-affine structure in this family of complex Hadamard matrices.
conclusion: The work clarifies the intersection of block-reducible forms and hypocycloid constraints and may support future searches for mutually unbiased bases in six dimensions, though it is a narrow mathematical contribution.

title: Long-Baseline Phase-Coherent Microwave Reception Using Rydberg Atoms
authors: Brook Feyissa Darmindra Arumugam
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A long baseline phase-coherent microwave receiver is demonstrated using a remotely interrogated cesium Rydberg atom sensor over an 8 m free-space optical link. A 3.989 GHz local oscillator (LO) is intensity-modulated onto an 852 nm optical probe and recovered remotely for atomic superheterodyne detection. A 509 nm coupling laser establishes a Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) system addressing the 6S1/2 to 6P3/2 to 56D5/2 ladder, with microwave coupling to 57P3/2. A test signal offset by 5 kHz generates an optically detected intermediate-frequency (IF) response returned to the reference station for centralized coherent acquisition. This eliminates independent remote oscillators, electronic IF acquisition, and distributed clock synchronization. Over 10 min, the differential phase between remote and local reference exhibits a standard deviation of 0.476 deg and a minimum overlapping phase Allan deviation of 0.048 deg at approximately 200 s averaging. Following optical-link interruption, the differential phase recovers without recalibration, with a measured pre- and post-interruption difference of 0.01 deg. These results demonstrate phase coherent remotely interrogated atomic microwave reception with reduced instrumentation, supporting future distributed interferometry, multistatic radar, and coherent sensor arrays.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a long-baseline phase-coherent microwave receiver using a remotely interrogated cesium Rydberg-atom sensor over an 8 m free-space optical link.
motivation: The authors aim to eliminate independent remote oscillators, electronic intermediate-frequency acquisition, and distributed clock synchronization in coherent microwave sensing arrays.
method: An intensity-modulated 852 nm optical probe is transmitted to a remote Rydberg-EIT sensor, where a 509 nm coupling laser and microwave fields produce an optically detected intermediate-frequency response returned to the reference station.
result: Over 10 minutes, the differential phase standard deviation is 0.476 degrees, with a minimum overlapping Allan deviation of 0.048 degrees near 200 s averaging, and phase recovery after link interruption differs by only 0.01 degrees.
conclusion: The work supports distributed interferometry, multistatic radar, and coherent sensor arrays by showing phase-coherent remotely interrogated atomic microwave reception with reduced instrumentation.

title: A Non-equilibrium Thermodynamics Formulation Of Shear Set-points In Adaptively Remodeling Vascular Networks
authors: Daniel P\'erez-Calixto Enrique Hern\'andez-Lemus
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Blood vessels remodel in response to wall shear stress while the network operates under a metabolic maintenance budget. For a power-law maintenance cost, minimizing dissipation at fixed budget yields a local shear set-point, and a purely local adaptation rule drives the network towards this optimum. Here we give this result a non-equilibrium thermodynamic formulation. Blood flow is an exactly linear Onsager system, and the slow remodeling of vessel radii is a gradient flow generated by a Rayleigh dissipation functional. This identifies the structural mobility, which scales inversely with the maintenance cost of each vessel and can be measured from radius fluctuations. Enforcing the budget exactly requires a time-dependent metabolic multiplier, which we obtain in closed form; with a fixed multiplier the budget is violated by up to one third during transients. The fluid displaced by remodeling vessels couples flow and structure through a symmetric, non-diagonal mobility, so that Onsager reciprocity becomes a testable statement: neighbouring vessels should show anticorrelated radius fluctuations. With noise, the structural sector obeys a second law and an integral fluctuation theorem. Non-reciprocal signaling between vessels, such as upstream conducted responses, then breaks the time-reversal symmetry of radius fluctuations and produces housekeeping entropy, detectable from time series of realistic length. Finally, we construct a partition function over network topologies with the number of loops as order parameter. Numerical tests show that loop counts do not collapse onto a single curve against an effective temperature, and that they depend strongly on the detection threshold.
tldr: The paper reformulates shear-stress set-points in adaptively remodeling vascular networks as a non-equilibrium thermodynamic theory with Onsager reciprocity, a Rayleigh dissipation gradient flow, and an integral fluctuation theorem for radius fluctuations.
motivation: Vascular networks remodel in response to wall shear stress under a metabolic maintenance budget; earlier work showed local adaptation rules converge to an optimal shear set-point, and the authors aim to embed this in a rigorous non-equilibrium thermodynamic framework.
method: Blood flow is treated as a linear Onsager system, slow radius remodeling as a gradient flow generated by a Rayleigh dissipation functional with a structural mobility tied to maintenance cost; a time-dependent metabolic multiplier enforces the budget, and stochastic noise yields a second law and fluctuation theorem for the structural sector, with non-reciprocal signaling producing housekeeping entropy.
result: A closed-form metabolic multiplier is derived (fixed multiplier violates the budget by up to one third in transients); Onsager reciprocity predicts anticorrelated radius fluctuations between neighboring vessels, and a partition function over network topologies with loop number as order parameter shows loop counts fail to collapse onto a single curve versus effective temperature and depend strongly on detection threshold.
conclusion: The framework provides testable thermodynamic signatures (anticorrelated fluctuations, housekeeping entropy from time series) for vascular remodeling, but the topological partition-function analysis reveals limitations of a simple effective-temperature description.

title: The Cost Of A Real Grover Oracle: Minecraft Seed Search From Software To Quantum Hardware
authors: Evan M. Reeves, Elias Sopkin, Thomas A. Searles
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the resource estimation of how known-constant arithmetic changes the cost of a Grover oracle for Minecraft 1.13.1 seed recovery, an application of quantum search to procedural content generation. The oracle developed here combines a structure-placement predicate with a reversible inverse transform of the linear congruential generator for the 32-bit residual search. Reduced-width arithmetic, phase marking, uncomputation, and complete Grover loops are verified against an independent Java reference, while production-width circuits are structurally audited. Direct Fourier-basis constant arithmetic reduces the placement-predicate width from 6n+3 to 4n+3 qubits and the structural scaling of the two-qubit gate counts from Theta(n^3) to O(n^2). Under backend-agnostic common-basis Qiskit level-0 {u, CX} accounting, the representative nonzero-r folded residual-search construction uses 275 circuit qubits, 48,896 CX gates, and depth 4,482, versus 467 qubits, 2,038,804 CX gates, and depth 186,328 for the original register-to-register baseline. Multi-placement conjunctions expose a width-recomputation tradeoff, and exact enumeration identifies a plateau in candidate reduction for the benchmark. We executed reduced-width placement circuits within complete Grover loops on IBM processors and Quantinuum H2-1 and show larger one-iteration increases in marked-state probability for the specialized construction than for the baseline. These results quantify the resource benefits of arithmetic specialization and show substantial routing sensitivity in the reduced-width IBM hardware experiments. Together, the results quantify the effect of specializing known-constant arithmetic within a PCG-derived oracle and show that its compiled hardware behavior strongly depends on routing and execution context.
tldr: The paper estimates and experimentally tests resource costs for a specialized Grover oracle applied to Minecraft 1.13.1 seed recovery.
motivation: It aims to quantify how known-constant arithmetic specialization reduces the cost of a real Grover oracle from software-level construction to compiled quantum hardware execution.
method: The authors design a reversible oracle combining a structure-placement predicate with an inverse linear congruential generator transform, use Fourier-basis constant arithmetic, and benchmark reduced-width circuits on IBM processors and Quantinuum H2-1.
result: The specialized construction reduces qubit width from 467 to 275, CX count from 2,038,804 to 48,896, and depth from 186,328 to 4,482 in the representative folded residual-search case, while hardware experiments show routing-sensitive behavior.
conclusion: Arithmetic specialization can substantially reduce Grover-oracle resources, but compiled performance depends strongly on routing and execution context in this application-specific setting.

title: Fully Quantum Training Of Parametric Circuits With Quantum Hamiltonian Descent
authors: Leonardo Banchi Marco Burato
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parametric quantum circuits are usually trained by classical, local optimizers, which use the quantum computer only to evaluate the cost function, or its gradient, one point at a time. Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) takes a different route: in this quantum algorithm for continuous optimization, the parameters become the position of a quantum particle, with the cost function as its potential, and two time schedules control kinetic and potential energy so that the wavefunction explores the whole landscape and tunnels towards the global minimum. QHD, however, assumes a classically computable cost function, and its digital implementation is poorly understood: standard error bounds grow exponentially with the number of qubits per parameter, and the schedules are borrowed from classical optimization. Here we propose to train parametric circuits with QHD entirely on the quantum computer, through an online step in which the qubits encoding the parameters coherently control the circuit on a second register. We prove that, for cost functions with a smooth periodic extension, including those of parametric circuits, the simulation error admits a bound independent of the grid resolution, and that for circuits the bound grows at most linearly with the number of parameters. We also show that the ideal dynamics depends on the two schedules only through a single curve, which controls the adiabaticity of the search, and that the remaining freedom can be used to minimize the gate count. Simulations on benchmark functions and parametric circuits show that, at equal cost, schedules designed in this way markedly increase the probability of finding the global minimum.
tldr: The authors propose training parametric quantum circuits entirely on a quantum computer using Quantum Hamiltonian Descent, where parameter qubits coherently control a second circuit register, and prove simulation error bounds independent of grid resolution and at most linear in the number of parameters.
motivation: Standard variational circuit training relies on classical local optimizers that query the quantum device point-by-point, while QHD assumes a classically computable cost function and suffers from exponentially growing digital-simulation error bounds and schedules borrowed from classical optimization.
method: An online fully quantum protocol in which the qubits encoding the continuous parameters coherently control the parametrized circuit on a second register, plus an analysis showing the ideal dynamics depend on the two time schedules only through a single adiabaticity-controlling curve, whose residual freedom is used to minimize gate count.
result: For cost functions with smooth periodic extensions (including those of parametric circuits) the simulation error bound is grid-resolution independent and grows at most linearly in the number of parameters; simulations on benchmark functions and parametric circuits show markedly higher global-minimum success probability at equal cost.
conclusion: Fully quantum QHD training of parametric circuits is a viable, resource-efficient alternative to classical optimizers, with provable error scaling and better empirical success rates.

title: Communication Complexity Of Integer Matrix Singularity
authors: Chengu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Alice and Bob hold complementary halves of the columns of an [MATH] matrix of [MATH]-bit integers and decide whether it is singular over [MATH]. Up to constant-factor dimension growth, this partitioned problem is equivalent to additive singularity, where Alice and Bob hold [MATH] matrices [MATH] of [MATH]-bit integers and test the singularity of [MATH] over [MATH]. We prove a bounded-error quantum lower bound [MATH] and a randomized upper bound [MATH]. The bounds match at [MATH] for [MATH]. The lower bound holds even under the promise of rank [MATH] versus [MATH]. Its proof combines an integer witness with a local digit encoding, while the upper-bound protocol lifts modular kernel relations using short messages. Bitwise sharing changes how the communication complexity depends on the entry bit length [MATH]. If Alice and Bob instead hold [MATH] matrices [MATH] of [MATH]-bit integers and test whether their entrywise bitwise XOR [MATH] is singular over [MATH], we prove a quantum lower bound [MATH], matching the trivial upper bound. This lower bound holds even under the promise of rank [MATH] versus [MATH]. Our proof uses a dense weighted equation and a signed Fourier witness whose exceptional dyadic frequencies can be removed at small variation cost.
tldr: The paper establishes matching quantum and randomized communication-complexity bounds for deciding the singularity of integer matrices held in complementary pieces by two parties.
motivation: Matrix singularity over the integers is a fundamental algebraic problem, and its communication complexity under partitioned and bitwise-shared input models is not well understood, particularly with respect to the entry bit length.
method: The authors prove a bounded-error quantum lower bound via an integer witness combined with a local digit encoding, and construct a randomized protocol that lifts modular kernel relations through short messages; a bitwise-XOR variant is handled with a dense weighted equation and a signed Fourier witness.
result: The quantum lower bound and randomized upper bound match for a range of parameters, and for the bitwise-XOR formulation a quantum lower bound matching the trivial upper bound is proven, even under rank promises.
conclusion: The work clarifies how bitwise sharing alters the dependence of communication complexity on entry bit length and settles the complexity of these integer-singularity problems up to the given parameters.

title: Partial Information Decomposition When Some Sources Are Known: A Source Chain Rule And A No-Go Theorem
authors: Aaron J. Gutknecht
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Partial information decomposition (PID) splits the information that several sources carry about a target into atoms, distinguished by which collections of sources give access to them. We ask how such a decomposition should behave when some of the sources are already known. The access structure of the atoms suggests one answer: discard the atoms that the known sources provide and regroup the rest according to which further sources unlock them. The classical construction of conditional information suggests another: recompute the decomposition under the conditional distributions and average. We show that the two answers agree, atom by atom, exactly when redundant information obeys a source chain rule, an analogue of the chain rule of mutual information: when the same sources are added to several collections, the enlarged collections share everything the added sources provide and, beyond that, exactly what the original collections share once the added sources are known. The rule divides established measures of redundant information, so that adopting or rejecting it genuinely narrows the choice of measure. Our main result is a no-go theorem: for three or more sources, the source chain rule and local positivity, the requirement that all atoms be nonnegative, cannot hold together in any PID.
tldr: The paper analyzes partial information decomposition (PID) under conditioning on known sources, proposes a source chain rule for redundant information, and proves a no-go theorem showing it is incompatible with local positivity for three or more sources.
motivation: PID aims to decompose the information multiple sources carry about a target into atoms, but it is unclear how the decomposition should behave when some sources are already known; two natural constructions—access-structure regrouping and conditional recomputation—motivate a source chain rule.
method: The author compares the access-structure approach with the conditional-distribution approach, identifies a source chain rule as the exact condition for their atom-by-atom agreement, and then proves a no-go theorem for three or more sources.
result: The source chain rule is shown to divide existing measures of redundant information, and the main theorem establishes that for three or more sources the source chain rule and local positivity cannot both hold in any PID.
conclusion: Adopting or rejecting the source chain rule meaningfully constrains the choice of redundancy measure, and the incompatibility result highlights a fundamental limitation of PID frameworks beyond two sources.

title: Study Of Localization Properties Under Subsystem Periodic Driving
authors: Arpita Goswami, Ranjan Modak, Shaon Sahoo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodic driving provides a powerful route for controlling localization and engineering effective Hamiltonians in quantum systems. A localized one-dimensional Aubry-Andr\'e chain can be driven into a fully delocalized phase when the entire system is driven below a critical frequency. Here, we ask whether such delocalization can be achieved by driving only a part of the system. We address this question using a two-leg ladder comprising an Aubry-Andr\'e chain coupled to a periodically driven clean tight-binding chain. Exact numerical calculations show that, starting from a localized static ladder, subsystem driving below a critical frequency cannot achieve complete delocalization. Instead, a mixed phase emerges, with localized and delocalized states coexisting and the fraction of delocalized states varying nonmonotonically with the driving frequency. This behavior can be understood using local effective Hamiltonians. Although these effective Hamiltonians are derived analytically in the high-frequency regime, they can nevertheless predict the localization transition occurring in the moderate-frequency regime. In fact, by quantifying the emergent nonlocality of the Floquet Hamiltonian, we show that these effective Hamiltonians provide a valid description up to a crossover frequency that is lower than the critical frequency associated with the localization transition. Our results demonstrate an alternative route to Floquet engineering, in which the transport properties of a quantum lattice system can be modified by driving only a subsystem.
tldr: The paper studies whether driving only part of a localized Aubry-André ladder can delocalize the full system and finds a mixed localized-delocalized phase rather than complete delocalization.
motivation: Periodic driving can control localization and engineer effective Hamiltonians, but it is unclear whether driving only a subsystem can achieve the full delocalization seen under global driving.
method: The authors use exact numerical calculations on a two-leg ladder with an Aubry-André chain coupled to a periodically driven clean tight-binding chain, and analyze local effective Hamiltonians and Floquet-Hamiltonian nonlocality.
result: Subsystem driving below a critical frequency does not produce complete delocalization; instead, localized and delocalized states coexist, with the delocalized fraction varying nonmonotonically with driving frequency.
conclusion: Subsystem driving offers an alternative Floquet-engineering route to modify transport, but effective high-frequency Hamiltonians remain valid only up to a crossover frequency below the localization transition.

title: Trial-space Co-design For Quantum Simulation On Noisy Hardware
authors: Bo Peng, Vibin Abraham, Himadri Pathak
