abstract: ArXiv:2610.33361v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An operator who positions mobile resources before a disruption faces two uncertainties that are usually treated as one: how the joint state of demand and travel conditions will vary, and which part of the resulting cost the positioning decision can actually change. Standard distributionally robust optimization (DRO) protects total cost, and therefore spends much of its protection on disruption costs that every feasible design would pay. This paper evaluates the worst-case regret of a design and compares it with the worst-case premium of total-cost DRO, and shows that the regret-to-premium ratio can be bounded before any robust model is solved: from marginals for the dependence question, and from single-scenario optima and one transport linear program for the regret question. The worst-case law is a relabelling of the operating record, reassigning every recorded period wholesale to another recorded period, except at most one, which is split. The comparator that exposes the largest worst-case regret is found by a single mixed-integer program. We derive an explicit radius where the sample-average design is exactly regret-robust. For finite scenario and design sets we compute a design's worst-case regret exactly, bound it from quantities a planner already has, and show on fleet and EMS data how law-relative regret changes capacity and positioning choices relative to sample-average and worst-cost planning. We apply the decision tree to several years of New York fleet data, including the year before Hurricane Sandy, and to two emergency-service events. The test flags the pre-Sandy year as exposed. The training-support regret bounds cover realized test regret in three of four fleet folds. On Ida, where the regret-robust allocation differed from the sample-average one, it moved units toward the boroughs the storm loaded and cost less than the sample-average design.
tldr: The paper proposes a regret-robust optimization framework for pre-positioning mobile resources under demand and travel-condition uncertainty, arguing that protecting worst-case regret rather than worst-case total cost isolates the portion of disruption cost that a design can actually influence.
motivation: Standard distributionally robust optimization spends much of its protection budget on disaster costs that are unavoidable for any feasible design, so the authors aim to separate 'how the joint state varies' from 'what the decision can change'.
method: Worst-case regret is evaluated against the worst-case premium of total-cost DRO, with the regret-to-premium ratio bounded a priori from marginals, single-scenario optima, and one transport linear program; the worst-case law is a relabelling of the operating record and the worst comparator is found by a mixed-integer program.
result: An explicit robustness radius where the sample-average design is exactly regret-robust is derived, and experiments on New York fleet data (including the pre-Sandy year, flagged as exposed) and EMS events show that training-support bounds cover realized test regret in three of four fleet folds, with regret-robust allocation for Hurricane Ida moving units toward the loaded boroughs at lower cost.
conclusion: Regret-based robustness yields materially different and often cheaper capacity and positioning decisions than sample-average or worst-cost planning, and can be certified from quantities a planner already possesses.

title: Coordinate Systems And Maximal Order Complexity In Banach Lattices
authors: A. Avil\'es, C. Rosendal, M. A. Taylor, P. Tradacete
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We resolve three questions arising from the study of coordinate systems and order convergence in Banach lattices. Firstly, every order (respectively, [MATH]-order) basis [MATH] for a Banach lattice [MATH] is automatically a Schauder basis. In fact, the associated partial sum projections satisfy a maximal inequality, and hence every such basis is uniform. Secondly, we show that there is a separable Banach lattice [MATH] in which the set $[MATH][MATH]^1_1[MATH]Y[MATH]Y^{\uparrow\infty}[MATH]^1_1[MATH]X_{\downarrow0}[MATH]Y^{\uparrow\infty}$ can be described in any simpler way than by the nonexistence of positive lower and upper bounds, respectively.
tldr: Pure functional analysis paper resolving three open problems about coordinate systems (order bases) and order convergence in Banach lattices.
motivation: The authors aim to settle questions left open in the theory of coordinate systems and order convergence in Banach lattices, in particular whether order bases are automatically Schauder bases and how certain order-limit sets can be characterized.
method: Abstract Banach lattice theory: analysis of order bases, M-order bases, partial sum projections and maximal inequalities, plus a constructive separable Banach lattice counterexample.
result: Every order (and M-order) basis of a Banach lattice is shown to be a Schauder basis, indeed a uniform basis satisfying a maximal inequality; a separable Banach lattice is constructed showing that certain order-convergence sets admit no simpler description than the absence of positive lower/upper bounds.
conclusion: The results clarify the interplay between order structure and topological (Schauder) basis structure in Banach lattices, closing three open questions in the area.

title: An Improved Fast Iterative Moment Method For The Simulation Of Near-continuum Gas Flows With Shakhov Model
authors: Zhenning Cai, Zhicheng Hu, Guanghan Li, Chunwu Wang, Xiaowen Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The fast iterative moment (FIM) method developed in [G. Li, C. Wang, and Z. Hu, Comput. Fluids, 311 (2026), 107031] achieves fast convergence for near-continuum gas flows modeled by the Boltzmann-BGK equation through alternating iterations between the high-order moment system and the consistent hydrodynamic equations. In this paper, we extend the FIM solver to the Shakhov model and improve it in the following aspects. A finite volume method with linear reconstruction is employed for high-resolution spatial discretization of both systems. Following the original FIM method, an implicit-explicit scheme treating the Shakhov collision term implicitly is adopted for the high-order moment system. A local Fourier analysis of a linearized one-dimensional BGK model reveals the need for more hydrodynamic iterations at smaller Knudsen numbers and their slower convergence on refined grids. Motivated by these findings, a Newton-multigrid method with a new regularization strategy is introduced for the hydrodynamic equations, generally providing an effective hydrodynamic correction with one step per alternating iteration, thereby reducing the need for empirical tuning. Numerical experiments for planar Couette flow, lid-driven cavity flow, and heat transfer in a bottom-heated cavity are carried out to investigate the performance of the improved FIM solver. The results demonstrate improved efficiency and robustness over the original FIM method, particularly at small Knudsen numbers, and favorable performance with both first- and second-order spatial discretizations.
tldr: The paper improves the fast iterative moment (FIM) method for simulating near-continuum gas flows governed by the Shakhov kinetic model.
motivation: The original FIM solver converges slowly and requires empirical tuning at small Knudsen numbers; extending it to the Shakhov model and accelerating hydrodynamic correction is needed for efficient rarefied-flow simulation.
method: A finite-volume discretization with linear reconstruction is applied to both the high-order moment system and the hydrodynamic equations; the Shakhov collision term is treated implicitly via an implicit-explicit scheme, and a Newton-multigrid method with a new regularization strategy is introduced for the hydrodynamic correction, guided by local Fourier analysis.
result: Numerical tests on planar Couette flow, lid-driven cavity flow, and bottom-heated cavity heat transfer show improved efficiency and robustness over the original FIM, particularly at small Knudsen numbers, for both first- and second-order spatial discretizations.
conclusion: The improved FIM solver provides a more efficient and robust approach for near-continuum gas-flow simulation with the Shakhov model, reducing empirical tuning needs.

title: Learning Representative Port Subsets For Efficient Fluid Antenna Systems
authors: Ming Zeng Quan Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fluid antenna systems (FASs) provide many candidate ports, but probing all ports for each channel realization incurs substantial online overhead. We study a complementary offline problem: compress the candidate-port space once and reuse the compressed set across future channel realizations. The method collects optimal ports from sampled training realizations, requiring only one scan of the candidate ports per realization. On a DeepMIMO 7-by-7 FAS with 49 candidate ports, 120 training realizations yield 27 representative ports on average while retaining 99.995% of the channel power gain achieved by exhaustive port selection.
tldr: The paper proposes an offline method to compress the candidate-port space of fluid antenna systems into a small representative port subset that can be reused across channel realizations, drastically reducing online probing overhead.
motivation: Fluid antenna systems offer many candidate ports, but exhaustively probing all ports for every channel realization creates substantial online overhead, motivating a one-time offline compression of the port space.
method: Optimal ports are collected from sampled training channel realizations (one scan of candidate ports per realization) and compressed into a representative port set that generalizes to future realizations.
result: On a DeepMIMO 7-by-7 FAS with 49 candidate ports, 120 training realizations yield 27 representative ports on average while retaining 99.995% of the channel power gain of exhaustive port selection.
conclusion: Offline port-subset learning offers an efficient, reusable alternative to per-realization exhaustive port probing in fluid antenna systems.

title: Tracer: An RDC-Triggered Trajectory Recovery Framework For Cyberattack-Resilient Adaptive Cruise Control
authors: Yicheng Yang, Tianyu Liu, Omar Tahri, Haoli Zhao, Yongfeng Dong, Tianyi Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The increasing connectivity of adaptive cruise control (ACC) systems exposes vehicle-state information to cyberattacks, potentially causing irrational car-following behavior and unsafe longitudinal dynamics. Existing trajectory recovery methods generally lack an interpretable criterion for recovery activation and remain vulnerable to attack-induced distribution shifts. To address these challenges, this paper proposes TRACER, a rational driving constraint (RDC)-triggered trajectory recovery framework for cyberattack-resilient ACC systems. TRACER employs a rationality-aware triggering (RAT) mechanism that activates recovery when the observed driving state violates the calibrated RDC bounds. It also introduces cross-branch robust imitation learning (CRIL), which combines a clean branch for learning nominal driving behavior with a noise-enhanced branch for improving robustness to corrupted observations. Cross-branch fine-tuning further aligns the robust recovery policy with the nominal driving-state distribution. Experiments across six cyberattack scenarios show that TRACER achieves reliable recovery triggering and outperforms state-of-the-art recovery baselines in terms of accuracy, stability, and safety. State-space analysis further confirms that TRACER mitigates attack-induced distribution shifts and restores coupled spacing-velocity dynamics, highlighting the effectiveness of robust policy learning for cyberattack-resilient ACC.
tldr: TRACER is a trajectory-recovery framework that detects cyberattacks on adaptive cruise control systems via a calibrated 'rational driving constraint' trigger and restores safe car-following behavior with cross-branch robust imitation learning.
motivation: Increasing connectivity of ACC systems exposes vehicle-state information to cyberattacks, causing unsafe longitudinal dynamics, and existing recovery methods lack interpretable activation criteria and degrade under attack-induced distribution shift.
method: The authors combine a rationality-aware triggering (RAT) mechanism that activates recovery when observed driving states violate calibrated RDC bounds with cross-branch robust imitation learning (CRIL), which pairs a clean nominal-behavior branch with a noise-enhanced branch and cross-branch fine-tuning.
result: Across six cyberattack scenarios, TRACER triggers recovery reliably and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in accuracy, stability, and safety; state-space analysis shows it mitigates distribution shift and restores coupled spacing-velocity dynamics.
conclusion: Robust policy learning with interpretable, constraint-based triggering offers an effective route to cyberattack-resilient adaptive cruise control.

title: Hidden Backdoor Attack On Deep Contrastive Clustering
authors: Zifeng Zhou, Shengda Zhuo, Jiahui Huang, Zeyan Li, Jinchun He, Peipeng Yu, Wangjie Qiu, Zhiming Zheng, Shuqiang Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep contrastive clustering has become a representative paradigm for unsupervised image clustering, yet its security under training-time poisoning remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates a hidden backdoor threat against deep contrastive clustering and proposes HBDCC, a Hidden Backdoor attack for Deep Contrastive Clustering. Here, hidden does not indicate that the trigger is visually imperceptible, but rather that the malicious trigger-cluster association remains behaviorally dormant on clean inputs and is activated only when the trigger appears at inference time. HBDCC poisons only a small fraction of unlabeled training samples and exploits an inherent structural weakness of contrastive clustering: augmentation-persistent triggers can be repeatedly aligned across different views at the instance level and further reinforced by cluster-level consistency objectives. As a result, the poisoned model preserves normal clustering behavior on clean data, while producing severely distorted cluster assignments for triggered inputs. We provide a dual-level analysis of the backdoor implantation mechanism and evaluate HBDCC on ImageNet-10, ImageNet-Dogs, and STL-10 with representative contrastive clustering frameworks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HBDCC can substantially degrade triggered clustering performance in a dataset-dependent manner while maintaining sufficient clean-data utility to evade standard evaluation protocols. We further conduct comprehensive studies on poisoning ratio, attack scope, trigger type, trigger size, and a lightweight knowledge-distillation-based mitigation strategy.
tldr: The paper proposes HBDCC, a training-time poisoning backdoor attack that implants a dormant trigger-cluster association in deep contrastive clustering models, degrading clustering only when a trigger is present at inference.
motivation: Deep contrastive clustering is a leading unsupervised image clustering paradigm, but its robustness to training-time poisoning and backdoor threats has been largely unexplored.
method: HBDCC poisons a small fraction of unlabeled training data with augmentation-persistent triggers that get repeatedly aligned across views at the instance level and reinforced by cluster-level consistency objectives, supported by a dual-level analysis of the implantation mechanism.
result: Experiments on ImageNet-10, ImageNet-Dogs, and STL-10 across representative contrastive clustering frameworks show severe degradation of triggered clustering while clean-data utility is preserved well enough to evade standard evaluation, with ablations on poisoning ratio, attack scope, trigger type/size, and a knowledge-distillation-based mitigation.
conclusion: Contrastive clustering carries a structural vulnerability to hidden backdoors, motivating dedicated defenses beyond standard clean-data evaluation protocols.

title: Spoofing The Toolbox: Optimizing Tool Descriptions To Deceive Llm Agents
authors: Shih-Chieh Dai, Xinyu Sun, Guanhong Tao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are widely used in many applications and often rely on external tools. Tool information, such as function descriptions, helps agents determine which tools best suit a given context. However, attackers can manipulate this information to mislead LLM agents into using malicious tools. Prior attacks mainly rely on keyword-based techniques, which are easily detected, or rule-based methods, which have limited effectiveness. In this work, we introduce TSA, a stealthy tool-spoofing attack that crafts descriptions for malicious tools that are difficult to distinguish from those of existing benign tools. To achieve this, we propose an LLM-powered optimization method that iteratively refines malicious tool descriptions. Specifically, TSA begins with a variant of a benign tool description and updates it based on feedback from a surrogate LLM agent. The optimization method incorporates a feedback function and contrastive in-context learning to guide the search for descriptions that are both stealthy and effective. Experiments on both single- and multi-tool use benchmarks demonstrate that TSA achieves an attack success rate of up to 92.13\%, outperforming four state-of-the-art approaches while remaining highly stealthy. Our user study further shows that even human participants cannot distinguish descriptions generated by TSA from benign ones. Moreover, TSA remains effective against five tool-malware detectors.
tldr: TSA is an LLM-powered optimization attack that crafts stealthy malicious tool descriptions to trick LLM agents into invoking attacker tools.
motivation: Existing tool-spoofing attacks against LLM agents rely on keyword-based tricks that are easily detected or rule-based heuristics of limited effectiveness, so a stealthier and stronger attack is needed to expose real vulnerabilities.
method: The authors start from a variant of a benign tool description and iteratively refine it using feedback from a surrogate LLM agent, combining a feedback function with contrastive in-context learning to jointly optimize for stealth and attack success.
result: TSA achieves up to 92.13% attack success on single- and multi-tool benchmarks, outperforming four state-of-the-art baselines, evades five tool-malware detectors, and fools human participants in a user study.
conclusion: Tool descriptions constitute a practical and hard-to-detect attack surface for LLM agents, motivating description-level defenses and provenance checks beyond keyword or rule filtering.

title: Deletion, Substitution, Repair And Transplant: Component Attribution In Barbican, A Layered Prompt-Injection Gateway For Mcp
authors: Edip G\"um\"u\c{s} \.ipek Abas{\i}kele\c{s} Turgut
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A neural classifier can fail completely inside a layered defense without any end-to-end number moving. We demonstrate this on BARBICAN, a fail-closed gateway for language-model tool mediation whose arbitration stage spent an entire recorded evaluation receiving text mangled by a misconfigured tokenizer. Correcting the misconfiguration lifts that stage's corpus-wide area under the ROC curve (AUC) from 0.392 to 0.855 and pushes system recall down, from 80.67% to 80.34%; a stub that answers "malicious" scores 80.77%, higher than either. The reason emerges once the stage's input distribution is examined: upstream routing hands it a band that is 96.82% malicious, and the enforcement design lets an incriminating verdict block while an exculpating one releases an input only through one narrow branch. Yet deleting it costs 673 detections. Substituting its verdict with a constant instead moves between 12 and 140 of 25,000 decisions. Transplanted into the arbitration stage, an off-the-shelf classifier that separates the band's inputs at an AUC of 0.916 changes 16 of 25,000 decisions. Measured against such detectors with operating points chosen away from the test data, the gateway leads on its own benchmark distribution and falls behind once that distribution changes. In our earlier gateway, the review model's band is 92.94% malicious and a constant verdict is as accurate as the review model. We argue that an ablation figure for any routed stage is unreadable without the class balance of the band that stage receives, and that deletion experiments need substitution experiments beside them.
tldr: BARBICAN is a layered fail-closed gateway for mediating language-model tool calls, and the paper shows that component ablations of its routed classifier stages are misleading unless the class balance of each stage's input band and substitution experiments are also reported.
motivation: Neural classifiers inside layered security defenses can silently fail—or appear useless in ablations—while end-to-end metrics stay flat, so the authors want a principled way to attribute component value in routed pipelines.
method: They instrument each stage of the BARBICAN prompt-injection gateway, correcting a tokenizer misconfiguration, then run deletion, constant-substitution, and transplant experiments (including an off-the-shelf classifier with AUC 0.916) over 25,000 decisions while tracking the per-stage malicious fraction.
result: Fixing the tokenizer lifts the arbitration stage's AUC from 0.392 to 0.855 while system recall slightly drops; deleting the stage costs 673 detections, whereas substituting a constant verdict or transplanting a stronger detector changes only 12–140 and 16 of 25,000 decisions respectively, because the routed band is 96.82% malicious.
conclusion: The authors argue that ablation numbers for routed stages are unreadable without the receiving band's class balance, and that deletion experiments must be paired with substitution experiments.

title: A-ge: Privacy-Preserving Age Assurance Via Fine-Grained Motion
authors: Mohammed Gharib, Giovanni Cascone, Martin Zizi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Age assurance faces a fundamental privacy dilemma: meaningful assurance typically requires revealing identity or other sensitive information, whereas privacy-preserving alternatives often provide little assurance. Existing approaches either disclose sensitive information directly or shift the disclosure and trust requirement to an identity provider, while self-declared age provides little meaningful assurance. Thus, a fundamental gap remains between establishing an age property and revealing information beyond what is necessary to establish that property. We present (Age-Grounded Evidence), a privacy-preserving age assurance system that derives age-related evidence from fine-grained motion captured by commodity inertial measurement units (IMUs). A-GE exploits subtle motion dynamics that we hypothesize reflect underlying neuromuscular and physiological processes during ordinary device interaction. It requires neither identity information nor government identification and operates across available sensor sampling rates, including the approximately 60~Hz limit of web-based sensing, with configurable minimum-age thresholds ranging from 14 to 21 years. We evaluate A-GE on more than 600 participants, with separate participant-disjoint cohorts for model development and final evaluation. At a 16-year minimum-age threshold, A-GE achieves up to 93.8\% accuracy with a comparable F1 score across the evaluated configurations. We further demonstrate client-side deployment on Android, iOS, and the web, and examine unintended attribute inference and residual privacy risks, characterizing both the privacy benefits and limitations of deriving age evidence from commodity motion.
tldr: A-GE is a privacy-preserving age-assurance system that infers age brackets from fine-grained IMU motion signals collected during ordinary device interaction, avoiding identity disclosure.
motivation: Age verification inherently trades privacy for assurance: identity-based checks over-disclose sensitive data, identity-provider schemes shift trust, and self-declaration offers no real assurance, leaving a gap between proving an age property and revealing unnecessary information.
method: The authors extract subtle motion dynamics from commodity inertial measurement units at sensor sampling rates down to roughly 60 Hz web sensing, hypothesize these reflect neuromuscular/physiological traits, and train participant-disjoint models with configurable minimum-age thresholds from 14 to 21 years, deploying client-side on Android, iOS, and web.
result: On over 600 participants with disjoint development and evaluation cohorts, A-GE reaches up to 93.8% accuracy with comparable F1 at a 16-year threshold, and the authors further characterize unintended attribute inference and residual privacy leakage.
conclusion: Commodity motion sensing can provide meaningful, privacy-preserving age evidence without identity data, though residual inference risks remain and define the practical limits of the approach.

title: Alignment Of Autonomous Cyber Defense Agents Via Adaptive Policy Shaping
authors: Dena Mujtaba, Bharadwaj Ravichandran, Brian Hu, Arslan Basharat
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cybersecurity operators increasingly encounter sophisticated and fast-paced attacks, making autonomous cyber defense (ACD) a critical approach for supporting timely and effective decision-making. Reinforcement learning (RL)-based ACD agents have the ability to autonomously observe network states and take actions to defend and recover system assets, making them well suited for ACD. However, these agents often face critical trade-offs, such as improving network security while inadvertently degrading service availability or violating other operational priorities such as confidentiality and integrity, raising the core challenge of aligning agent behavior with human-specified goals and intent. In this work, we study the problem of aligning RL-based ACD agents with human-specified operational objectives without requiring costly retraining. We formalize alignment for ACD as a policy shaping problem, where a pretrained RL decision-making policy can be adjusted at test time using predicted attributes over agent actions. We also propose an adaptive approach that dynamically controls the alignment--performance trade-off as operational priorities shift during an ongoing cyber attack. We evaluate our method in a simulated cyber defense environment, CybORG, analyzing performance across multiple alignment objectives using the Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA) information security triad. Our results show that adaptive test-time policy shaping can significantly improve alignment while preserving core cyber defense performance, offering a practical and scalable alternative to training-time alignment methods in RL. Our code is publicly available at [URL].
tldr: The paper proposes adaptive test-time policy shaping to align pretrained reinforcement-learning cyber-defense agents with human-specified operational objectives such as confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
motivation: RL-based autonomous cyber defense agents face trade-offs between security and service availability, and retraining them to match shifting human intent is costly, so a cheaper alignment mechanism is needed.
method: Alignment is formalized as a policy-shaping problem in which a pretrained RL policy is adjusted at test time using predicted attributes over actions, with an adaptive controller managing the alignment-performance trade-off as priorities change.
result: Experiments in the CybORG simulated cyber-defense environment show that adaptive test-time policy shaping substantially improves alignment on CIA-triad objectives while preserving core defense performance.
conclusion: Adaptive test-time policy shaping is presented as a practical, scalable alternative to training-time alignment for RL agents in cyber defense.

title: Secure And Functional Code Generation With Self-Evaluation
authors: Gias Uddin Md Afif Al Mamun
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code that remains insecure. Security-focused fine-tuning can be expensive and is not always available, motivating inference-time approaches. Security-oriented prompting and retrieval can reduce vulnerabilities, but may also remove required behavior or apply defenses incompatible with the task. The challenge is to identify relevant security knowledge and use it to improve security without sacrificing functionality. We present SecGent, an inference-time framework that retrieves weakness context from the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) database and applies it to secure code generation. By connecting task specifications to relevant textual CWE records, SecGent provides task-specific security guidance without relying on retrieved vulnerable or patched code examples. Complementary functional and security tests check the resulting implementation, and their execution feedback guides repairs toward satisfying both objectives. We evaluate SecGent with four open-source LLMs and Claude Sonnet 5.5 across five programming languages on the CWEval benchmark. It achieves the highest joint functional--security success against four inference-time baselines for all five models. Across the open-weight models, mean functional-security@1 (FS@1) improves by 15.5% over RAG, with gains in both functionality and security, and by 19.8% over the strongest prompt optimizer compiled for each model. On Sonnet, FS@1 reaches 92.1%, outperforming the strongest baseline AutoGen by 4.8%. In a separate comparison, SecGent outperforms Claude Code with security-focused prompting by over 6% in FS@1. Feedback-guided repair further improves FS@1 by up to 6.7% over generation without feedback, primarily by recovering functionality while checking security.
tldr: SecGent is an inference-time framework that retrieves CWE weakness descriptions to guide LLM-based code generation toward jointly functional and secure outputs, validated by both functional and security tests.
motivation: LLMs often produce functionally correct but insecure code, and security-focused fine-tuning is costly; existing security prompting or retrieval methods can break required functionality or apply incompatible defenses.
method: The framework links task specifications to relevant textual CWE records (avoiding retrieval of vulnerable/patched code examples), generates code under task-specific security guidance, and uses execution feedback from complementary functional and security tests to drive repairs.
result: Across four open-source LLMs and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in five languages on CWEval, SecGent achieved the best joint functional-security success versus four inference-time baselines, with FS@1 gains of 15.5% over RAG and 19.8% over the strongest prompt optimizer; feedback-guided repair added up to 6.7%.
conclusion: Retrieving and applying task-specific security knowledge at inference time, combined with dual functional/security test feedback, improves secure code generation without sacrificing functionality.

title: More Meters Or More Prices? One- Vs. Multi-dimensional Fee Mechanisms On Ethereum
authors: Fei Wu, Maria In\^es Silva, Stefanos Leonardos, Carmine Ventre
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Permissionless blockchains use transaction fee mechanisms to allocate the resources that transactions consume, such as execution, data bandwidth, and state creation. Recent blockchain designs explore pricing these resources separately rather than through a single unit. We study this shift on Ethereum, whose roadmap moves in stages from a one-dimensional fee mechanism to a multi-dimensional one. We build a demand model for the three resources, calibrated from Ethereum's 2025 block-capacity increases, and find that state creation is the most price-responsive. We then evaluate both mechanisms at higher block capacity, combining the model with transaction-level metering reconstruction and block-level simulation. Under a one-dimensional mechanism, state creation determines the fee and suppresses execution throughput. Adjusting how state is metered can align resource usage under constant demand, but a single fee cannot track all resources when demand varies, leaving all underutilized. A multi-dimensional mechanism removes this fee coupling, but execution still generates data that must be propagated. Across different allocations between block execution and propagation time, the multi-dimensional mechanism delivers 4--34\% more execution throughput at similarly low congestion, with higher target utilization and state growth near its intended level.
tldr: The paper compares one-dimensional versus multi-dimensional transaction fee mechanisms on Ethereum, showing that multi-dimensional pricing yields 4–34% more execution throughput at similarly low congestion.
motivation: Ethereum's roadmap is moving from a single-unit fee mechanism to separately pricing execution, data bandwidth, and state creation, but the consequences of this shift for throughput and resource utilization were not well understood.
method: The authors build a demand model for three resources calibrated from Ethereum's 2025 block-capacity increases, combine it with transaction-level metering reconstruction and block-level simulation, and evaluate both mechanisms at higher block capacity.
result: Under a one-dimensional mechanism, state creation dominates the fee and suppresses execution throughput, and a single fee cannot track all resources when demand varies; the multi-dimensional mechanism removes this coupling and delivers 4–34% more execution throughput with higher target utilization and state growth near its intended level.
conclusion: Multi-dimensional fee mechanisms are preferable for Ethereum's scaling path, though execution still generates data that must be propagated, so block execution and propagation time allocations matter.

title: ProbeID: Verifying Mcp Tool Identity For Llm Agents Under Registry Drift
authors: Guanxing Chen, Sining Zhang, Haohuai He, Qiujie Lv, Yu-An Huang, Zhi-An Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents select tools by copyable descriptions, which cannot establish which implementation runs. ProbeID compares canonicalized responses to schema-valid probes with a trusted admission reference and abstains on ambiguity, so a squatter must copy probe-observable behavior. With the gold present, independent probes and a fixed margin, standard concentration arguments give a shared probe budget logarithmic in the candidate count and bound the joint probability of a wrong decision. On cached MCP-IdentityDrift cases, strict choice reaches \(0.956\) hit@1 while description routers fall near chance, but simpler exact comparisons tie it, MMD better tolerates heavy value noise, and a 32B behavioral judge is similarly accurate at higher cost. Random probes from agent banks and a prospective held-out study of 38 tools test theory-set thresholds. On the agent banks, equality refuses every reachable replacement from 64 probes and the bounded distance from 512, and sharper post hoc gates halve both. Two tools whose drift no bank probe reaches always pass. In an MCP-Bench agent, verification cuts tainted tasks from 15 to 9 of 16 at unchanged task success. Over eleven weeks, 7 of 59 real tools changed responses despite version pins. Verification depends on reference integrity, probe coverage, and response noise.
tldr: ProbeID verifies which implementation of an MCP tool an LLM agent actually invokes by comparing canonicalized responses to schema-valid probes against a trusted admission reference, abstaining under ambiguity.
motivation: Agent tool selection relies on copyable descriptions that cannot establish which implementation actually runs, so a malicious 'squatter' tool can impersonate a legitimate one, especially as registries drift over time.
method: The authors design probe-based behavioral fingerprinting with canonicalization, independent probes, and a fixed decision margin; concentration arguments bound the shared probe budget logarithmically in candidate count and bound the joint wrong-decision probability, with comparisons against exact-equality, MMD, and LLM-judge baselines.
result: Strict choice reaches 0.956 hit@1 on cached MCP-IdentityDrift cases while description routers perform near chance; on agent banks equality rejects every reachable replacement with 64 probes and bounded distance with 512, and verification reduces tainted tasks from 15 to 9 of 16 at unchanged task success, though two drift cases remain undetectable and 7 of 59 real tools changed responses over eleven weeks despite version pins.
conclusion: Behavioral probe verification is practical for securing LLM agent tool use, but its guarantees depend on reference integrity, probe coverage, and response noise.

title: A Factor-6 Truthful-in-Expectation Mechanism For Cascade Position Auctions
authors: Baao Xie Qiuyu Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Position auctions require assigning advertisers to positions and determining their display order. Under cascade behavior, earlier clicks prevent users from reaching later placements, coupling the click probabilities of selected advertisements. Existing methods achieve constant-factor welfare approximation and monotone logarithmic-factor approximation separately, leaving open whether both guarantees can be attained simultaneously. The difficulty is that welfare-preserving rounding need not maintain the monotonicity of individual click-through rates required for truthful bidding. We resolve this problem by developing a polynomial-time randomized mechanism that achieves a factor-6 welfare approximation and truthfulness in expectation for arbitrary public advertiser-position click probabilities. The mechanism optimizes a reach-weighted linear relaxation and converts its solution into feasible ordered allocations through matching decomposition, probability-bounded grouping, and calibrated attenuation. This construction compensates for cascade dependence and ensures that each advertiser's expected click-through rate equals exactly one sixth of its fractional click coordinate. The resulting identity transfers the monotonicity of the fractional allocation to the implemented mechanism, enabling exact incentive-compatible payments while preserving the welfare guarantee. The allocation lottery and payments are computable in polynomial bit time, with exact sampling in expected polynomial time.
tldr: The paper presents a polynomial-time randomized mechanism for cascade position auctions that simultaneously achieves a factor-6 welfare approximation and truthfulness in expectation.
motivation: Existing cascade position auction mechanisms obtain either constant-factor welfare approximation or monotone logarithmic-factor approximation, but not both simultaneously, because welfare-preserving rounding can break the monotonicity of click-through rates needed for truthful bidding.
method: The authors optimize a reach-weighted linear relaxation and convert the fractional solution into feasible ordered allocations via matching decomposition, probability-bounded grouping, and calibrated attenuation, ensuring each advertiser's expected CTR equals one sixth of its fractional click coordinate.
result: The construction transfers monotonicity from the fractional allocation to the implemented mechanism, yielding exact incentive-compatible payments while preserving the factor-6 welfare guarantee, with allocation and payments computable in polynomial bit time.
conclusion: The mechanism closes the open question of whether welfare approximation and truthfulness in expectation can coexist in cascade position auctions, at the cost of a factor-6 loss.

title: Ranking Is Not Deciding: Benchmark Shortcuts And Operating-Point Collapse In Query-Time Rag Poisoning Defenses
authors: Arvin Sahaym Pushkal Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Query-time filters that screen each retrieved document before it reaches the generator are the dominant published defense against retrieval-augmented generation poisoning, and they report near-perfect detection on domain benchmarks. We show that this performance is predicted by how the poison set was built rather than by what the filter reads: removing a single construction cue destroys the deployed decision before it destroys the ranking. Two label-free statistics of a poison set and its clean corpus profile the cue: containment, how often the target question appears verbatim in the poison, and length overlap. PoisonedRAG's released code prepends the target question to every inserted passage. Of the 21 published defense evaluations we survey, 8 verifiably run poison built this way and 5 substitute a length cue; separately, 12 report no false-positive rate at the operating point they deploy. Deleting only that prefix from the attack authors' own passages (0.93 still retrieved for their target) takes RAGuard, a published content filter we re-implement, from AUROC 0.953 to 0.758 and its miss rate from 0.191 to 0.763. Across four corpora, four attack families and ten per-document defenses on one shared candidate set, the profile predicts where detection saturates. Padding medical poison to clean length with word-shuffled filler that carries no content takes TrustRAG's set-level stage from a miss rate of 0.000 to 0.827, and one learned scorer of ours from 0.000 to 0.986 (0.321 at a matched 5% false-positive rate) while its AUROC holds at 0.953. The ranking survives; the decision does not. A defense-aware attacker defeats our own scorer, so we claim no defense. A detection result is evidence only when it is reported with its poison set's construction profile and the false-positive rate at the threshold actually deployed; we release the script that computes the profile.
tldr: The paper shows that near-perfect detection reported by query-time RAG poisoning defenses is largely an artifact of poison-set construction cues (verbatim question prefixes, length overlap) rather than genuine content discrimination, and that removing those cues collapses operating-point decisions while ranking metrics survive.
motivation: Published per-document filters against retrieval-augmented generation poisoning claim near-perfect detection on domain benchmarks, and the authors argue this performance reflects how the poison set was built rather than what the filter actually reads.
method: The authors define two label-free statistics of a poison set and clean corpus (containment of the target question verbatim, and length overlap), survey 21 published defense evaluations for these cues and for reported false-positive rates, and re-run defenses such as RAGuard and TrustRAG across four corpora, four attack families and ten per-document defenses on a shared candidate set after stripping the cue.
result: Deleting only the prepended question prefix drops RAGuard from AUROC 0.953 to 0.758 and its miss rate from 0.191 to 0.763; padding poison to clean length raises TrustRAG's set-level miss rate from 0.000 to 0.827 and a learned scorer's from 0.000 to 0.986 while AUROC holds at 0.953.
conclusion: Detection results should be reported with the poison set's construction profile and the false-positive rate at the actually deployed threshold; the authors release a script to compute this profile and explicitly claim no defense of their own since a defense-aware attacker defeats their scorer.

title: CVE-to-ATT&CK Mapping Via Evidence-Constrained Ranking
authors: Kai Wei, Yuwen Cui, Kehan Shen, Guangjing Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mapping CVEs to MITRE ATT&CK techniques helps defenders translate vulnerability information into hypotheses about adversary behavior. Automating this mapping is challenging because relevant evidence is fragmented across heterogeneous security sources. In addition, ATT&CK techniques can be semantically similar, and existing annotations cover a highly long-tailed subset of the technique space. Existing supervised, retrieval-based, and LLM-based approaches therefore face limitations from closed-set supervision, semantic ambiguity, or unconstrained prediction. We formulate CVE-to-ATT&CK mapping as multi-evidence constrained ranking. Our framework TRACE first integrates complementary structural and semantic evidence from multiple sources to construct a bounded, high-coverage candidate pool over the complete ATT&CK technique space. It then reranks the retained candidates by combining their accumulated evidence with CVE--technique textual interactions and frequency-aware scoring. We evaluate the framework across six public datasets with different annotation processes and vulnerability distributions. Candidate construction reduces the 201-technique ATT&CK search space by approximately 60% while retaining at least one ground-truth technique for 95.11%-100% of CVEs. These results show that combining heterogeneous security evidence with constrained ranking provides a more controlled and generalizable bridge from vulnerability information to adversary behavior.
tldr: TRACE is a framework that maps CVE vulnerability records to MITRE ATT&CK techniques by building a bounded, high-coverage candidate pool from heterogeneous security evidence and then reranking candidates with evidence-weighted, frequency-aware scoring.
motivation: Defenders want to translate vulnerability data into hypotheses about adversary behavior, but automating CVE-to-ATT&CK mapping is hard because evidence is fragmented across sources, techniques are semantically similar, and annotations are long-tailed, which breaks closed-set supervised, retrieval-based, and unconstrained LLM approaches.
method: The authors formulate the task as multi-evidence constrained ranking: structural and semantic evidence from multiple security sources constructs a candidate pool over the full 201-technique ATT&CK space, which is then reranked using accumulated evidence, CVE-technique textual interactions, and frequency-aware scoring.
result: Across six public datasets with differing annotation processes and vulnerability distributions, candidate construction shrinks the ATT&CK search space by about 60% while retaining at least one ground-truth technique for 95.11%-100% of CVEs.
conclusion: Combining heterogeneous security evidence with constrained ranking yields a more controlled and generalizable bridge from vulnerability information to adversary behavior than prior closed-set or unconstrained approaches.

title: Back To Basics: Formal Analysis Hints Improve Weak-to-Strong Monitoring
authors: Daniel Ben-Levi, Judah Goldfeder, Mateusz Dziemian, Raja Moreno
abstract: ArXiv:2610.34064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier agentic systems are capable of taking misaligned actions that may cause significant harm. Monitoring techniques are developed to oversee these systems in order to detect and prevent dangerous actions. However, current state-of-the-art monitors suffer from four persistent failure modes: complete detection failures, partial detections, accepting false benign framings, and suspicion score calibration errors. These failure cases can be efficiently combated by augmenting transcripts with supplementary hints, spanning command provenance, security-sensitive action flags, and task-disallowed effect markers. Provenance links allow for the recognition of diffuse attacks, while security and authorization flags simultaneously enable subtle attack recognition and provide an explicit reason for monitors to doubt the false benign framings they encounter, reducing rationalization and improving calibration. We find that augmenting weak extract-and-evaluate monitors with these hints significantly boosts performance with minimal computational cost. Furthermore, a failure mode analysis confirms that hints can remediate all four failure modes, notably almost entirely eliminating detection failures. A series of ablation studies emphasizes the efficiency and potential of the augmented extract-and-evaluate approach. Synthesizing our findings, we propose a tractable two-pronged approach toward enabling weak-to-strong monitoring.
tldr: This paper proposes augmenting transcripts with supplementary hints—command provenance, security-sensitive action flags, and disallowed-effect markers—to improve weak-to-strong monitoring of frontier agentic AI systems.
motivation: State-of-the-art monitors for detecting misaligned actions by frontier agentic systems suffer from four persistent failure modes: complete detection failures, partial detections, acceptance of false benign framings, and poor suspicion-score calibration.
method: The authors augment weak extract-and-evaluate monitors with structured hints spanning command provenance, security/authorization flags, and task-disallowed effect markers, then conduct failure-mode analysis and ablation studies to assess efficiency and effectiveness.
result: Hint augmentation significantly boosts monitoring performance at minimal computational cost, remediating all four failure modes—notably nearly eliminating complete detection failures—while ablations confirm the efficiency of the augmented extract-and-evaluate approach.
conclusion: The authors propose a tractable two-pronged approach toward enabling reliable weak-to-strong monitoring of agentic AI systems, based on inexpensive formal-analysis hints embedded in transcripts.

title: Some Remarks On Polynomial Vector Fields In $\rr^2$
authors: Soumen Sarkar Supriyo Jana
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study planar polynomial vector fields admitting invariant circles. We characterize polynomial vector fields having [MATH] concentric invariant circles, and we describe those having three invariant circles whose centers are not collinear. We also give a necessary and sufficient condition for the unit circle to be the unique limit cycle of a quadratic vector field. We prove that a cubic or quartic Kolmogorov vector field having the unit circle invariant has no circular limit cycle, and that a quartic vector field with two concentric circular limit cycles has at most three circular limit cycles, this bound being sharp.
tldr: The paper studies planar polynomial vector fields with invariant circles and circular limit cycles.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize polynomial vector fields admitting multiple invariant circles and to bound circular limit cycles in low-degree Kolmogorov systems.
method: The analysis uses algebraic characterization of invariant circles, center conditions, and limit cycle criteria for quadratic, cubic, and quartic polynomial vector fields.
result: They characterize fields with concentric invariant circles, give a condition for the unit circle to be the unique limit cycle of a quadratic field, and prove sharp bounds on circular limit cycles for cubic and quartic Kolmogorov fields.
conclusion: The work contributes to classical planar dynamical systems and Hilbert-type limit cycle problems, with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Hybridizable Discontinuous Galerkin Methods For The Keller-Segel Model
authors: Silvia Bertoluzza, Gabriella Bretti, Micol Pennacchio, Christophe Prud'homme
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) finite element method to approximate the solution of the time-dependent Keller-Segel model, a drift-diffusion system describing chemotactic cell movement. We develop and analyze the corresponding HDG scheme, and establish theoretical convergence results for the proposed discretization. Finally, we present numerical experiments that confirm the theoretical findings.
tldr: The paper develops and analyzes a hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin (HDG) finite element scheme for the time-dependent Keller-Segel chemotaxis drift-diffusion system.
motivation: The Keller-Segel model describes chemotactic cell movement via coupled drift-diffusion equations, and robust high-order numerical schemes with provable convergence are needed to simulate such systems accurately.
method: The authors formulate an HDG finite element discretization of the time-dependent Keller-Segel equations and carry out a theoretical convergence analysis of the scheme.
result: Theoretical convergence results are established for the proposed discretization, and numerical experiments are presented that confirm the predicted convergence behavior.
conclusion: The HDG method provides a theoretically sound and numerically validated approach for approximating chemotaxis drift-diffusion dynamics.

title: The Intersection Of Nested Filled-in Little Julia Sets Have Zero Area
authors: Carsten Lunde Petersen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33328v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is shown that for any infinitely renormalizable quadratic polynomial [MATH] the intersection [MATH] of all the little filled-in Julia sets (renormalization Julia sets) containing the critical value have zero area.
tldr: The paper proves that for infinitely renormalizable quadratic polynomials, the intersection of all little filled-in Julia sets containing the critical value has zero area.
motivation: The work addresses a structural question in complex dynamics about the geometry of nested renormalization Julia sets.
method: The proof uses renormalization theory for quadratic polynomials and analyzes the nesting of filled-in Julia sets around the critical value.
result: For any infinitely renormalizable quadratic polynomial, the intersection of all such little filled-in Julia sets is shown to have zero planar area.
conclusion: This establishes a measure-theoretic rigidity property of the nested renormalization structure in quadratic complex dynamics.

title: Joint Service Depth And Priority Design In Queueing Systems
authors: Adam N. Elmachtoub, Yash Kanoria, Jonathan Y. Tan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In AI-assisted service systems, the server can choose how much processing effort to spend on each job, which we call the service depth. Deeper reasoning improves output quality but occupies the server longer and increases congestion, and the realized processing time remains random because AI models are probabilistic and tasks vary in complexity. We study the joint design of service depth and priority in a single-server queue whose customers differ in delay sensitivity, with the goal of maximizing social welfare. For each customer type, the decision maker chooses a priority level and a service depth, and service times are exponential with mean equal to the chosen depth. With two customer types and linear service values, we characterize the centralized optimum. Counterintuitively, it prioritizes the patient type and gives it a smaller service depth when patient customers are sufficiently prevalent. When delay sensitivity is private, however, incentive compatibility requires the impatient type to receive a weakly shorter sojourn time, so the optimal price menu never prioritizes the patient type. Consequently, there can be a welfare gap between the centralized decision maker's optimal control policy and the optimal decentralized pricing mechanism. With a continuum of types, the centralized optimum is monotone: more delay-sensitive customers receive weakly smaller depth and higher priority, so the optimum can be implemented by a price menu with no welfare loss. Allowing randomized depths similarly closes the gap in the two-type model. Finally, we calibrate an agentic AI service system using published coding-agent trials from DeepSWE and numerically examine priority inversion, the value of joint design, and the welfare gain from personalization.
tldr: This paper studies joint design of service depth (processing effort) and priority in a single-server queue with heterogeneous, delay-sensitive AI-service customers, maximizing social welfare.
motivation: AI-assisted service systems can choose how much reasoning effort to spend per job; deeper processing improves quality but increases congestion, so the design of service depth and scheduling priority must be treated jointly.
method: Queueing-theoretic analysis of exponential service times whose means equal chosen depths, characterizing centralized optima for two types and a continuum of types, plus incentive-compatible price-menu design under private delay sensitivity, with numerical calibration to coding-agent trials.
result: The centralized optimum can counterintuitively prioritize the patient type with smaller depth; under private information, incentive compatibility forbids this, creating a welfare gap that vanishes for a continuum of types or with randomized depths.
conclusion: Joint service-depth and priority design matters, and pricing mechanisms can match centralized optimal control in richer type spaces, yielding gains from personalization in agentic AI service systems.

title: From Caveman To Coba: Coordinated Optimization-Based Attacks On Grid-Edge Smart Inverters In DER-Rich Power Systems
authors: Emad Abukhousa, Anna Raymaker, Animesh Chhotaray, Daniel Molzahn, Saman Zonouz, Sakis Meliopoulos
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33401v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aggregation platforms and smart-inverter control channels can allow a compromised coordination layer to alter active- and reactive-power commands across a geographically distributed DER fleet. This paper introduces the Coordinated Optimization-Based Attack (COBA), which uses network information and location-specific DER P/Q setpoints to maximize thermal loading on a selected transmission corridor. COBA is compared with low-information CAV baselines limited to a single uniform fleet command: all-off, all-on, maximum reactive absorption, or maximum reactive injection. The Hawaii Synthetic Grid-37 Buses case is evaluated with rooftop-photovoltaic-like capability aggregated at 20 selected 69-kV buses and verified using MATPOWER power flow. Under the case's single-reference-bus balancing convention, COBA overloads B86 (WAIALUA69-WAIANAE69) near 30% penetration and B51 (COCONUT69-PALM69) near 55%, while same-target uniform loadings remain lower and uniform commands primarily stress other natural weak lines. The results show that topology, target selection, and command capability determine DER-induced thermal risk beyond aggregate penetration alone.
tldr: The paper introduces COBA, a coordinated optimization-based cyberattack that manipulates smart-inverter active and reactive power setpoints to overload targeted transmission corridors in DER-rich power grids.
motivation: Aggregation platforms and smart-inverter control channels create attack surfaces where a compromised coordination layer could issue coordinated DER commands, but the risk beyond aggregate DER penetration is not well characterized.
method: The authors formulate a Coordinated Optimization-Based Attack using network information and location-specific DER P/Q setpoints, compare it against low-information uniform CAV baselines, and evaluate it on the Hawaii Synthetic Grid-37 Buses case with MATPOWER power-flow verification.
result: COBA overloads specific lines near 30% and 55% DER penetration, while uniform fleet commands remain less effective on the same targets and primarily stress other naturally weak lines.
conclusion: Topology, target selection, and command capability determine DER-induced thermal risk, so aggregate penetration alone is insufficient for assessing grid-edge smart-inverter attack impact.

title: A Model-Theoretic Formalization Of AlKhwaremis Ilm Alfaraid
authors: Elnaserledinellah Mahmoud Abdelwahab
abstract: ArXiv:2610.33629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a model theoretic and computational formalization of AlKhwarizmis treatment of inheritance within the framework of Computational Fiqh. We first show that every inheritance configuration in a specified class is representable as a finite system of rational linear equalities and inequalities, and that such systems are decided exactly by Fourier Motzkin elimination over Q. We then define the fixed dimensional inheritance structure Vd with distinguished claimant coordinates, and prove that every admissible rational linear coordinate realization is isomorphic to Vd, this establishes the algebraic representation as canonical within that class. The complete first order theory Td of Vd is shown to be complete by construction and is explicitly distinguished from the decidability of the inheritance relevant fragment. The methodological principle is then related to a broader formalization of closed Fiqh domains via exhaustive case generation, Horn clause axiomatization, and terminating deduction, yielding domain relative computational completeness.
tldr: The paper formalizes Al-Khwarizmi's Islamic inheritance (Ilm al-Faraid) rules using model theory and computational logic, showing inheritance configurations form rational linear systems decidable by Fourier-Motzkin elimination.
motivation: The author aims to extend 'Computational Fiqh' by giving a rigorous model-theoretic and algorithmic account of classical inheritance jurisprudence, establishing canonicity and completeness for the resulting structures.
method: Inheritance configurations are encoded as finite systems of rational linear equalities and inequalities, decided via Fourier-Motzkin elimination over Q; a fixed-dimensional structure V_d with claimant coordinates is defined and its first-order theory T_d is analyzed for completeness, alongside Horn-clause axiomatization and terminating deduction.
result: Every admissible rational linear coordinate realization is shown isomorphic to V_d, making the algebraic representation canonical; the complete first-order theory T_d is proven complete by construction and distinguished from decidability of the inheritance-relevant fragment.
conclusion: The work yields domain-relative computational completeness for closed Fiqh domains, demonstrating that exhaustive case generation plus Horn-clause axiomatization and terminating deduction can formalize such legal reasoning systems.
